💡 Key Takeaways
  • President Donald Trump appears to have responded to the dramatic midterm results by doubling down on MAGA.
  • While Trump will still need to be more cooperative and responsive toward the Democratic Congress, and in some cases will have no choice, Miller’s elevation will certainly push back against what should be the natural rhythm of presidential politics: When the president’s party suffers a whopping midterm defeat, and that president is a lame duck struggling with major domestic and international challenges, he moves toward the center.
  • Industry observers note that president Donald Trump appears to have responded to the dramatic midterm results by doubling down on MAGA.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Get audio access with any FP subscription.

President Donald Trump appears to have responded to the dramatic midterm results by doubling down on MAGA. Among his first major acts after the blue wave was replacing his trusted chief of staff, Susie Wiles, with Stephen Miller. Few moves could have signaled more clearly that Trump the fighter was not going to give way to Trump the conciliator. Because the White House chief of staff is often considered the second most powerful position in Washington, the choice carries particular weight. Miller has been seen as one of the most influential voices in Trump 2.0, if not the most influential. He has been the driving force behind an extraordinarily expansive view of presidential power: targeting what the administration considers opposition institutions such as law firms, the media, and universities; launching a sweeping detention and deportation program; imposing a tariff program that rocked the national economy; and making aggressive moves in Latin America that have included striking boats allegedly transporting illegal narcotics.

While Trump will still need to be more cooperative and responsive toward the Democratic Congress, and in some cases will have no choice, Miller’s elevation will certainly push back against what should be the natural rhythm of presidential politics: When the president’s party suffers a whopping midterm defeat, and that president is a lame duck struggling with major domestic and international challenges, he moves toward the center.

Industry observers note that president Donald Trump appears to have responded to the dramatic midterm results by doubling down on MAGA. Among his first major acts after the blue wave was replacing his trusted chief of staff, Susie Wiles, with Stephen Miller. Few moves could have signaled more clearly that Trump the fighter was not going to give way to Trump the conciliator. Because the White House chief of staff is often considered the second most powerful position in Washington, the choice carries particular weight. Miller has been seen as one of the most influential voices in Trump 2.0, if not the most influential. He has been the driving force behind an extraordinarily expansive view of presidential power: targeting what the administration considers opposition institutions such as law firms, the media, and universities; launching a sweeping detention and deportation program; imposing a tariff program that rocked the national economy; and making aggressive moves in Latin America that have included striking boats allegedly transporting illegal narcotics.

While Trump will still need to be more cooperative and responsive toward the Democratic Congress, and in some cases will have no choice, Miller’s elevation will certainly push back against what should be the natural rhythm of presidential politics: When the president’s party suffers a whopping midterm defeat, and that president is a lame duck struggling with major domestic and international challenges, he moves toward the center.

But that’s not how Miller thinks, nor has it been Trump’s instinct. The Miller appointment stands in sharp contrast to the personnel change that then-President Ronald Reagan, the founding father of the conservative movement, made after the 1986 midterms and the scandal that broke out soon after. That year, Democrats regained control of the Senate (they had held the House since 1955), and the administration was embroiled in a major scandal that some Democrats believed could reach Watergate-like levels.

Industry observers note that the contrast between these two presidents reveals just how far Republican politics has radicalized since the 1980s. It is also a warning sign for Republicans who understand that, without a major course correction, the very same party that was celebrating a latest governing coalition in 2024 might be on a self-destructive path. The GOP is in the grip of a strong leader who is not particularly interested in the long-term health of the party that brought him to the White House.

Sources indicate that reagan was not enjoying a good political moment in November 1986, though his presidency had been riding high until then. His first term was highly successful, featuring a historic supply-side tax cut and a vast acceleration of defense spending. He had defeated his opponent, former Vice President Walter Mondale, in a landslide victory in 1984. His approval ratings had been strong, and the economy had recovered from the malaise of the 1970s. In October 1986, Reagan signed bipartisan tax reform legislation that closed loopholes benefiting some of the nation’s most powerful interests, and he held a historic summit with the new Soviet leader, Mikhail Gorbachev.

But then came the 1986 midterms. Democrats gained five seats in the House, expanding their majority to 258, and, more importantly, retook control of the Senate by gaining eight seats. Their 55-seat majority ended the brief period of Republican control that had started with the 1980 election. The outcome was seen as a rebuke of the harsher edges of U.S. conservatism, as well the heightened tension with the Soviet Union that a hawkish Reagan had helped spur, despite two summits with Gorbachev. Indeed, the summit just weeks before voting in Reykjavik, Iceland, had broken down because the president refused to give up on his initiative to build a missile shield around the United States, the Strategic Defense Initiative (which opponents dismissed as “star wars”). Soon after the election, Reagan’s problems deepened as news spread that a Lebanese magazine had reported that the United States had been secretly selling weapons to Iran.

One of Reagan’s most significant moves in early 1987 was to replace his highly controversial chief of staff, Donald Regan. A former Marine and chairman of Merrill Lynch, Regan had been an notable part of the Reagan administration since January 1981. As secretary of the Treasury, he had been instrumental in passing the 1981 tax cut. In February 1985, he became chief of staff, replacing James Baker (who replaced him at Treasury). Regan proved to be a forceful presence. He centralized control and pushed the president’s program in a highly aggressive and abrasive fashion that angered colleagues in the White House, as well as on Capitol Hill. The media did not find him very pleasant to work with, while first lady Nancy Reagan didn’t trust that he prioritized her husband’s interests.

It has been revealed that with Regan by his side, Reagan’s first public response to what became the Iran-Contra scandal was defiance, which reflected his chief of staff’s approach to most concerns. On Nov. 13, Reagan went on television to insist that there was nothing serious to investigate. While acknowledging that the White House had sold a small amount of “defensive” weapons to Iran as part of a major diplomatic initiative to build ties with moderates within the regime and combat terrorism, he denied that the United States had traded arms for hostages, or that the sales amounted to anything significant. Polls indicated that the public was unconvinced that the president was telling the whole truth. Then, on Nov. 25, the other shoe dropped: Attorney General Edwin Meese declared that profits from the weapons sales had been diverted to the anti-communist Nicaraguan Contras, despite the Boland Amendments’ congressional ban on such aid.

Sources indicate that privately, administration officials feared where the investigations were headed. For a generation that had watched Richard Nixon resign over Watergate just 12 years earlier, the possibility of impeachment seemed real. Reagan’s aides also understood that many voters had been shaped by those same memories, and were deeply distrustful of government officials and still insistent on a political system that could hold them accountable.

On Feb. 26, 1987, the president’s Special Review Board, a commission appointed by Reagan in November and headed by former Texas Sen. John Tower, issued its report on the Iran scandal. It blamed a chaotic management system that had allowed the arms sales and the diversion of funds to proceed, faulting Reagan’s leadership style and singling out Regan for failing to impose order on the White House. The next day, Regan resigned after learning that he was about to be relieved of his duties.

At this fraught moment, the president turned to Howard Baker.

In a recent development, the 61-year-old, mild-mannered Republican had served in the Senate from 1967 to 1985, the last four years as majority leader, and was respected on both sides of the aisle. He had been mentored by Senate Minority Leader Everett Dirksen (who was also his father-in-law), who taught him the ways and means of the legislative process and the art of bipartisan deal-making. Baker had gained national fame during the 1973 Watergate hearings by asking, “What did the president know and when did he know it?” Known as a moderate and an institutionalist, Baker was a selection widely seen as Reagan’s recognition that, with Democrats now controlling both chambers, he needed to build bridges to Capitol Hill rather than burn them. “I’d probably take some lumps from our right wingers but I can handle that,” Reagan noted in his diary, of appointing Baker.

Though Baker had actually been the third choice for chief of staff, he helped bring stability to the White House and guided the president through the Iran-Contra scandal. He brought in a first-rate team of advisors who improved relations with Congress, the press, and the first lady. Reagan biographers credit Baker with helping Reagan survive the scandal as the revelations mounted during the 1987 congressional hearings. He played a key role in brokering a budget deal with Congress after the October 1987 stock market crash and securing Senate ratification of the INF Treaty with the Soviet Union in May 1988. His tenure also had setbacks, most notably the Senate’s rejection of Robert Bork’s nomination to the Supreme Court. But his pragmatic outlook helped Reagan recover from the low of the 1986 midterms. “You always leave yourself a backdoor, a side door, and a trapdoor,” he liked to say, quoting something his father used to tell him. According to a longtime aide, that meant: “You don’t talk in absolutes. You don’t want to get yourself boxed in where you can’t maneuver.”.

Overall, Reagan and the first lady had reason to be pleased with Baker’s work: The president left office with high approval ratings—and helped bring an end to the Cold War.

Today’s Republican Party is not your grandfather’s Republican Party, and the recent midterms suggested that much of the electorate is not happy with it. The reach of the Democratic victories into deeply red parts of the country, including Mississippi, South Carolina, Texas, and Kansas, suggests that the onetime party of Lincoln has a major problem on its hands. Part of that problem is the president himself, who after further radicalizing the GOP to its electoral detriment, indicates few signs that he will change course in ways that could strengthen the party that brought him to the dance.

With Miller as chief of staff, Trump is assuring voters that there will be more of the same style of politics and the same political agenda—leaving the Democratic Party with the kind of political prospects for united government that seemed impossible just a few months ago.

Julian E. Zelizer is a columnist at Foreign Policy and a professor of history and public affairs at Princeton University. One way to read the tea leaves on the recent U.S. midterms is that, at long last, Washington gets serious about regulating artificial intelligence; the unchecked build-out of those wildly unpopular data centers is reconsidered; Significant Tech is held to account; and the United States becomes not just the most advanced AI power but also the more trustworthy AI power. But if you were expecting that the electoral “techlash” would lead to coherent AI governance, policy, and statecraft, then prepare to be disappointed. The more likely outcome is that we shall live with two more years of muddied U.S. technology policy at home and abroad, with one clear winner: Beijing.

For while Democrats did benefit from the promise of checking AI growth, and they now own the legislative machinery, the party must balance three competing impulses: to rein in AI, to ride the AI-led economic momentum and avoid economy-wide slowdowns before the 2028 elections, and to avoid ceding the AI leadership to China.

Sources indicate that one way to read the tea leaves on the recent U.S. midterms is that, at long last, Washington gets serious about regulating artificial intelligence; the unchecked build-out of those wildly unpopular data centers is reconsidered; Big Tech is held to account; and the United States becomes not just the most advanced AI power but also the more trustworthy AI power. But if you were expecting that the electoral “techlash” would lead to coherent AI governance, policy, and statecraft, then prepare to be disappointed. The more likely outcome is that we shall live with two more years of muddied U.S. technology policy at home and abroad, with one clear winner: Beijing.

For while Democrats did benefit from the promise of checking AI growth, and they now own the legislative machinery, the party must balance three competing impulses: to rein in AI, to ride the AI-led economic momentum and avoid economy-wide slowdowns before the 2028 elections, and to avoid ceding the AI leadership to China.

Industry observers note that to make gnarly matters more tangled, U.S. AI’s central player, Nvidia, has lost its co-founder and CEO over an alleged Chinese intelligence operation, scrambling all three impulses. And we should also remember that over at the White House, a bruised but belligerent Trump retains the executive levers and the veto—as well as an impulse to stymie whatever the Democrats wish to demonstrate as a “win” to the American public.

Before we get to Trump, though, let’s first consider what drives each of the camps in the Democratic coalition.

According to recent reports, the first camp can be thought of as the Restrainers. They want to check the proliferation of data centers while holding AI executives to account for independent testing of advanced models—and holding the companies liable for harm.

Midterm voters rewarded candidates in this camp, who pushed back on a sense that AI development was proceeding unchecked; Sherrod Brown won back an Ohio Senate seat with ads calling his opponent “the face of AI data centers,” while Jon Ossoff in Georgia and Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan also won races with opposition to data centers as a key element of their campaign platforms. In nine states, governors and governors-elect, too, have promised or imposed a pause on new data centers, stalling an estimated 41 percent of the country’s data center pipeline. Meanwhile, right after the elections, veteran Sen. Bernie Sanders called for a national data center moratorium.

According to recent reports, while slowing down AI would be the most readily available and popular move by lawmakers, the Restrainers still have to get their house in order. They will need to prioritize the many risks and concerns around AI and focus their limited time on the most significant ones. Weighing these will not be easy. A household worried about its power bill, for instance, needs a different intervention compared with a parent who doesn’t want their child left alone with a chatbot.

Recent findings suggest that A second camp is made up of the Riders. They have their eye on the economy and want to ensure that AI investments keep carrying U.S. growth, the stock market, and household retirement savings. AI has propped up the American economy in recent years; letting the air out of that balloon could produce a bust, a recession, and shrinking retirement accounts, which could be bad news come 2028 if voters lay the blame on Congress.

Recent findings suggest that the sharp Nov. 5 reminder about the connection between AI growth and stock market growth is hard to ignore—right after the midterms results had sunk in, the S&P 500 stock index fell 4.4 percent, its worst day since the April 2025 tariff shock, led by stocks tied to the data center build-out, while the Nasdaq also had its deepest one-day drop in 19 months, with investors worried about tougher AI rules from a Democratic Congress.

The Riders will urge caution: hold the hearings, pass disclosure rules, but don’t touch the capital spending contributing to the economy and the stock market. Several moderate Democrats, such as Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro or Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear, who are also presumed to be business-friendly, are considering presidential runs. They are likely to be the influential voices in the Riders camp.

As for the third camp, let’s call them the Racers. These are Democrats who prioritize national security concerns and want to keep sensitive technology and advanced chips away from adversaries. Specifically, they are eager to ensure that China not win the AI race. The Racers have support from the likes of influential senators such as Elizabeth Warren and Democratic leader Chuck Schumer as well as post-midterms in-the-spotlight senators including James Talarico.

While the AI race against China was not the matter that galvanized voters in the midterms and swept Democrats into Congress, a startling fresh development has the potential to make this a more pivotal political lever: the scandal involving Jensen Huang, who admitted to an affair with a woman alleged to be a Chinese spy. This puts a spotlight on the extent to which China is keen to compete and centers the geopolitical stakes of the AI race in voters’ minds.

In a recent development, huang’s abrupt exit from the company that he co-founded puts wind at the backs of the Racers, especially with curbing chip sales to China becoming a rare cause with bipartisan support. But it also pushes the other camps to revise their agendas.

Industry observers note that the Restrainers’ scrutiny of Big Tech’s leadership has national security implications. They will by now have realized that Nvidia did not have so much as a board chair until the day that Huang left—hardly a case for letting the industry police itself. For the Riders, with Nvidia as the load-bearer for the AI edifice, instability at the top could produce instability across the economy. They can point to half a trillion dollars of Nvidia’s market value being lost within a few days of the scandal breaking and the board investigation beginning.

Industry observers note that A Democratic coalition made up of these camps necessarily has a mix of divergent priorities. But while the legislative agenda will be set by political calculation, Congress can only guess at what a lame-duck president who controls the agencies, the veto, the export licenses, and his own stake in the AI trade will do in response.

Industry observers note that we have just had a preview: Even as a bipartisan chip bill is in process on Capitol Hill, the White House moved first, issuing its own rule to choke off China’s access to U.S. chips through data centers abroad.

In a recent development, the public will vote again in two years, too short for politicians and too long for technologists. With all these conflicting forces in motion, I would argue that Congress needs to allocate its limited bandwidth to a prioritized short list of AI risks, such as those recorded in my own register of 103 documented cases.

Sources indicate that in the absence of a reconciliation across the divergent camps, the result could be a U.S. AI build-out that advances in fits and starts as deals get negotiated, an export regime that can swing with each hearing, a standoff between legislators on Capitol Hill and the White House, and allies who hedge because they cannot predict U.S. policy.

In a recent development, the Chinese AI industry would be handed the perfect case for promoting itself to the world as the comparable, trustworthy, and cheaper alternative. And it has managed to get to this point even without access to the most advanced chips that Huang himself had wanted to sell to them.

According to recent reports, meanwhile, to win, Beijing will not need a newly ascendant Democratic Party to pick the wrong camp. It only needs Washington to pick none.

Bhaskar Chakravorti is the dean of global business at Tufts University’s Fletcher School of Law and Diplomacy. He is the founding executive director of Fletcher’s Institute for Business in the Global Context, where he established and chairs the Digital Planet research program. His next book Defeating Disinformation (co-edited with Joel Trachtman) will be published by Cambridge University Press in January 2025.

America Can Do Good—and Do Well

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 15 min read (2906 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foreignaffairs

⏱️ ~15 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • ANDREW NATSIOS was Administrator of the U.S.
  • Industry observers note that among all the ruinous consequences of the so-called U.S.
  • It has been revealed that no country can be a great power without a functioning foreign aid program.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

ANDREW NATSIOS was Administrator of the U.S. Agency for International Development and the President’s Special Envoy to Sudan during the George W. Bush administration. He is the author of Guns Are Not Enough: Foreign Aid in the National Interest, from which this essay is adapted.

The Strategic Logic of Foreign Aid.

Industry observers note that among all the ruinous consequences of the so-called U.S. Department of Government Efficiency’s efforts to cut bureaucracy, none has been as profound as the destruction of the United States’ ability to deliver foreign aid. A comprehensive Lancet study shows that the U.S. Agency for International Development’s assistance prevented more than 90 million deaths between 2001 and 2021. Using a mortality model, Boston University epidemiologist Brooke Nichols has estimated that the 2025 dismantling of USAID contributed to more than 700,000 excess deaths over roughly a year. A study published in Science this May found that after USAID’s shutdown, places that had lost large amounts of the agency’s assistance experienced a marked uptick in armed clashes and riots. The development economists Marcella Nicolini and Fabio Sabatini, meanwhile, demonstrated that economic activity in areas that formerly enjoyed substantial U.S. aid had dramatically declined.

It has been revealed that no country can be a great power without a functioning foreign aid program. But today, the United States does not have one. After 90 percent of USAID’s programs were terminated and 90 percent of its staff members were laid off, Congress formally reappropriated most of the budgetary funding dedicated to U.S. foreign aid. But the Office of Management and Budget (OMB) has not released all of this appropriated funding. More damaging still, USAID’s mechanisms for spending aid money have been dismantled. According to the Pew Research Center, annual U.S. foreign aid disbursements fell by $26 billion between the 2023–24 and 2024–25 fiscal years; $2.5 billion in appropriated funding designated for foreign aid went unspent by the end of the 2025–26 fiscal year.

According to recent reports, russell Vought, OMB’s director and a self-identified Christian nationalist, has stonewalled spending for programs related to supporting democracy and insisted that humanitarian grants can be sent only to two specific Christian nongovernmental organizations. U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio, meanwhile, unveiled that he wanted to end funding to USAID development contractors, universities, and local civil society organizations without understanding the downside of other options for aid dollars, such as budget support, which are far less accountable, uniquely American, and results-oriented.

Given the suffering created by the end of USAID, it is even more troubling that DOGE’s objectives to slash waste and boost transparency have not been realized. U.S. President Donald Trump’s 2025 “big beautiful bill” erased any modest savings won by DOGE’s cuts to foreign aid. And the decision to move USAID’s functions to the State Department, which has weak business systems and inadequate staff to manage aid programs, has thus far led to the transfer of $3.8 billion in U.S. foreign aid money to the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs and $15.9 billion directly into foreign governments’ treasuries through memorandums of understanding.

According to recent reports, these governments often have limited capacity to spend the money wisely and produce results. In the past, USAID’s Office of the Inspector General has harshly criticized such options because it is nearly impossible to audit the transfers. Over 90 percent of the countries involved in these agreements score below 50 (out of 100) on Transparency International’s Corruption Perceptions Index, indicating serious systemic corruption. This may explain why State Department political appointees have kept the texts of these health agreements secret.

It has been revealed that clashing demands—that aid should relieve misery abroad, that it ought to serve U.S. military and diplomatic interests, and that it ought to yield rapid, visible, and quantifiable results—always complicated the enterprise. And over the course of 65 years since USAID’s 1961 founding, overregulation, a centralization of control over programs, and congressional meddling created a rigid straitjacket that made the United States less responsive to local governments and local needs. But what the current U.S. administration didn’t understand was that USAID’s bureaucracy, so often presented as an obstacle to effectiveness, was in fact an adaptation to manage these conflicts.

Recent findings suggest that simply abolishing that institutional architecture with no strategy to replace it has only generated more confusion and waste. Meanwhile, China is racing to offer alternative sources of development financing, and Russia is seeking to expand its global influence through security partnerships. The United States cannot afford to let its foreign aid apparatus atrophy. It must redirect it, not reject aid.

Ever since USAID was created, the expectations that leaders in Washington had for foreign aid have conflicted with realities in the developing world, the way actual aid programs are managed, and the speed and nature of societal change. When I read through USAID’s 1960s-era archives to write my new book, I was struck that the demands early U.S. policymakers made of the institution were the same as those made today: policymakers wanted rapid, visible, and quantifiable results. Those demands were as unrealistic then as they are now. U.S. President John F. Kennedy hoped that poverty in Latin America would visibly recede within a couple of years of USAID’s creation, as he was understandably worried that the Cuban revolutionary leader Fidel Castro’s Marxist ideology was spreading across the region. Fourteen months after the organization’s inception, an article by Joseph Kraft in Harper’s Magazine reported that policymakers in Washington had already judged it a failure because it was not delivering “quick and visible results.” David Bell, USAID’s second administrator, recalled in 1965 that Kennedy had complained that the agency was “slow-moving, inefficient, and unresponsive to the President’s policy.”.

In a recent development, but diplomacy and development operate on profoundly different time horizons. Nearly all foreign aid programs have diplomatic consequences, even if they aren’t designed to. When diplomatic goals become the main or only goals of an aid program, however—for instance, when U.S. aid kept the Congolese dictator Mobutu Sese Seko in power during the Cold War—good development often fails.

The United States began institutionalizing foreign aid after World War II through agencies and programs such as the Marshall Plan, which supported the postwar economic recovery of Western Europe, and the Point Four Program, a Truman administration initiative to promote development in poor countries to reduce their susceptibility to communism. All along, policymakers debated whether U.S. assistance programs should principally aim to save lives and reduce extreme poverty or to support U.S. foreign policy by countering the influence of hostile powers.

In fact, USAID ended up playing a key role in winning the Cold War. American assistance strengthened governments targeted for Soviet and Chinese communist subversion, particularly in Asia. After U.S. President Richard Nixon entered his second year in office, aid spending for agriculture was increased to 50 percent of USAID’s budget and was directed primarily toward Asia. According to multiple studies by development economists, the effort saved more than 245 million lives. The green revolution, implemented over decades in Pakistan, India, Indonesia, the Philippines, South Korea, and Taiwan (among other countries), helped produce large grain surpluses that fueled industrialization and economic growth and averted the kind of famines that historically produce coups or mass uprisings.

Throughout this era, however, Washington’s demands that aid accomplish diplomatic goals—and quickly and visibly—also undermined the most crucial elements of development programs: institution building and policy reform. Strong institutions separate wealthy countries from poor ones. The former have them in abundance, while the latter do not. Institution building and policy reform should be the focus of aid programs. But institution building and policy reform is difficult to measure, takes many years to implement successfully, and is not immediately visible. Instead, policymakers insisted that USAID do service delivery, producing valuable humanitarian programs that were ultimately unsustainable.

In a recent development, most critical analyses of U.S. foreign aid conclude that USAID came to focus on process over substance, resulting in excessive bureaucracy. What these critiques overlook is what caused this obsessive focus on process. A web of federal regulatory and oversight agencies (what scholars call the counterbureaucracy) loosed on U.S. aid programs an army of federal auditors, accountants, regulators, compliance officers, and congressional staffers dedicated to reining in the bureaucracy and—supposedly—protecting taxpayers’ money. This onslaught slowed down USAID’s implementation of programs and created massive amounts of paperwork. It did not make aid programs more effective.

Industry observers note that historically, Congress ended up playing a particularly intrusive role in the management of U.S. foreign aid programs. USAID reported to 14 congressional committees, which often clashed, pulling USAID in different directions and slowing program implementation. (For example, the House and Senate agriculture committees, under the influence of the agriculture lobby, stonewalled efforts to reform food aid by insisting it be exported from the United States, while legislative appropriators and authorizers from foreign affairs committees strongly supported local purchase reform.) Congress also imposed intrusive earmarks—defined amounts allocated for specific programs, projects, or organizations. When countries asked for specific help, USAID often could not respond, because the glut of earmarks meant there was no discretionary money left.

Starting in the 1990s, the State Department attempted to exert more control over the USAID budget. A 1998 statute, for instance, made the USAID administrator report directly to the secretary of state. In January 2001, the State Department took control of USAID’s budget. That only led lawmakers—who often distrusted State—to add more earmarks. To protect U.S. foreign aid programs from an especially hostile Senate Foreign Relations Committee chairman, Republican Senator Jesse Helms, the Clinton administration instructed each cabinet-level department to create its own aid programs that would fall outside that committee’s jurisdiction. For example, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention at the Department of Health and Human Services established regional offices around the world, the Environmental Protection Agency developed solar energy projects in poor countries, and the Federal Emergency Management Agency signed agreements with more than 28 developing countries to assist in disaster management. USAID was already running programs such as these, yielding overlapping mandates which added to the incoherence of U.S. foreign aid.

Sources indicate that when I became USAID administrator in 2001, I discovered a foreign aid program whose funds were straitjacketed by nearly 250 congressional earmarks, a sum exceeding USAID’s total appropriation. At the time, Ethiopia was one of the most severely food insecure countries in the world. Yet in 2007 only 1.5 percent of USAID’s budget was devoted to agricultural development, 1.5 percent to economic growth, and 1.5 percent to governance reform; Congressional earmarks made it impossible to fund these programs to match the Ethiopian government’s request.

Recent findings suggest that despite all these impediments, foreign aid remained a critical component of U.S. foreign policy. The Department of Defense had a particularly productive partnership with USAID, recognizing that foreign aid could be as notable as force in incentivizing insurgents to make peace. The effects of USAID projects in Afghanistan were profound but took shape over long time horizons neither the State Department nor the Defense Department had any patience for. (USAID’s Afghanistan media-development program, for instance, was a great success, as documented in a Harvard Kennedy School study by The New York Times’s David Rohde.) Major academic studies have shown that in Iraq, community development projects undertaken by USAID’s Office of Transition Initiatives (OTI) employed large numbers of young men who might otherwise have been recruited into militias, reducing U.S. military casualties in the provinces with the highest levels of violence. In 2004, Army General Peter Chiarelli called the USAID officer managing the program, Kirk Day, a “hero” for saving his soldiers’ lives.

Industry observers note that the DOGE team abolished OTI last year, along with innumerable other programs that alleviated suffering globally and enhanced U.S. soft power. When Congress restored many cuts to foreign aid, it did not reinstate USAID’s veteran staff, historical archives, business systems, field presence, or implementing partner networks of universities, international nongovernmental organizations, local civil society groups, and international development contractors. The transfer of programs to the Department of State only exacerbated the contradictions that have long bedeviled U.S foreign aid. Few secretaries of state (or secretaries of defense) have any development background, experience, or technical knowledge, and paradoxically, when aid is seen simply as a tool of diplomacy or defense rather than an end in itself, the diplomatic good it can do is compromised.

According to recent reports, dismantling USAID did not abolish the need for technically knowledgeable staff and bureaucratic systems. In May 2025, the State Department inspector general issued an intimidating report detailing what the department will have to do to competently manage foreign aid programs, a list of demands it will have difficulty meeting. And in September this year, the Government Accountability Office issued a highly critical audit of the State Department’s inadequate management of foreign aid programs, finding that the department lacked documented standards for deciding which aid programs to terminate, could not produce data on its own staffing, and maintained incomplete or incorrect records on grants and agreements. This result was unsurprising, given that the State Department is a diplomatic policy institution, not a program management agency. Merging USAID into the State Department makes as much sense as merging Microsoft with ExxonMobil, given the disparate time horizons on which the two institutions operate and their differences in mission statements and business systems.

The State Department has pursued alternative arrangements for distributing aid that require less direct management. For example, it has negotiated 36 memorandums of understanding with governments in developing countries to transfer U.S. aid funds to their health ministries, so they can spend the program money themselves. But in return for these transfers, Washington has asked these countries to send private health-care data to the U.S. government, accept undocumented immigrants the U.S. government deports, and, in some cases, give U.S. mining companies access to their rare-earth minerals. Because health programs save lives, they should be distributed based on need, not on parochial, transactional American demands.

Many countries have understandably resisted this kind of bargain. USAID had technical staff that could assess a foreign government’s ability to manage funds responsibly. In practice, it ran a detailed and thorough vetting of nearly every aspect of the governments it partnered with. The State Department, by contrast, only vets according to the legal minimum and treats foreign governments as it treats as international or U.S.-based NGOs. State’s approach will increase the risk that funds are stolen by local government ministries that lack the control systems needed to ensure accountability.

Sources indicate that the very public and grossly inaccurate attacks on USAID’s integrity and management by Trump and DOGE’s erstwhile leader, Elon Musk, have damaged the agency’s reputation so extensively that simply resurrecting it will be difficult. But Washington’s aid apparatus also needs more coherent organization than it was afforded in the past. In his celebrated work Bureaucracy, on which my book is structured, the political scientist James Q. Wilson argues that strong U.S. departments or agencies need “relative autonomy”: clearly defined missions they do not substantially share with other agencies. By this logic, if the United States wants a high-functioning, coherent foreign aid program, it must first consolidate all aid functions within one department.

Industry observers note that abolishing field offices (called USAID missions) also made administering aid programs much more difficult, blunted true accountability and U.S. influence in the developing world, and reduced the visibility of U.S. aid programs. These country missions must be reestablished, reporting to the local U.S. ambassador. In Washington, Congress should create a new cabinet-level department reporting to the president that manages all the government’s aid programs, which would make it possible to trim staff, streamline program implementation, and avoid policy incoherence. At least 80 percent of this new department’s staff should be deployed abroad, not in Washington. The United States will always need to be able to launch aid programs with an expressly diplomatic purpose and short time horizon, and the State Department should determine these projects and their spending levels. But it should leave the programs’ management up to the new aid department—as it did during the Cold War, when USAID was independent of State.

This newly introduced department should also report to fewer congressional committees—a foreign affairs authorizing committee and an appropriations subcommittee in each legislative body. The practice of burdening the United States’ foreign aid budget with domestically appealing earmarks—which prevents aid from responding to foreign countries’ own needs—must be reduced.

In the past, the overregulation and bureaucratization of foreign aid driven by the demands of the counterbureaucracy prioritized process over programs and compliance over developmental outcomes. The upcoming aid department must be given regulatory relief. One way to do that is for Congress to set up charter missions, similar to charter schools, as an experiment to see whether accountability deteriorates. These deregulated charter missions would be free from burdensome reporting requirements the counterbureaucracy demands. In recent years, the World Bank has tried a similar approach and found that it improved its programs’ effectiveness without increasing fraud.

Recent findings suggest that the status quo for U.S. foreign aid cannot last. But Washington cannot revert to the old status quo, which generated the kind of dissatisfactions among policymakers that helped lead to its dismantling. Now is the time to bring more coherence to U.S. foreign aid programs with these reforms, if the fresh Democratic Congress and future administrations show a forward-looking vision.

The Case for a Trump-Xi-Putin Summit

  • In a recent development, in just a few days’ time, U.S.
  • These worries are entirely justified; Trump has a track record of cozying up to autocrats and turning his back on democratic allies.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, CHARLES KUPCHAN is Professor of International Affairs at Georgetown University and a Senior Fellow at the Council on Foreign Relations. He is the author of Bringing Order to Anarchy: Governing the World to Come.

In a recent development, in just a few days’ time, U.S. President Donald Trump, Chinese leader Xi Jinping, and Russian President Vladimir Putin could be holding a three-way summit on the sidelines of next week’s Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation meeting in Shenzhen, China. According to The Wall Street Journal, Putin floated the idea of a trialogue last month as an opportunity to discuss ending the war in Ukraine. No firm plan has yet been confirmed, but even the prospect of this meeting has provoked widespread consternation. Polish Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski warned against a repeat of the Yalta Conference of 1945, when U.S. President Franklin Roosevelt and British Prime Minister Winston Churchill capitulated to Soviet leader Joseph Stalin’s push for the Soviet Union to dominate Eastern Europe. U.S. Senator Chris Coons posted on X that “there can be no talks about Ukraine’s future without Ukraine at the table, and there can be no real negotiations as long as Trump signals weakness and servitude to Xi and Putin at every opportunity.”.

These worries are entirely justified; Trump has a track record of cozying up to autocrats and turning his back on democratic allies. Should he sit down with Xi and Putin, he must avoid selling out European and Asian partners who will not be at the table. And given the three leaders’ headstrong personalities and competing national interests that pit the United States against what Xi calls a “no limits” partnership between China and Russia, the meeting might ultimately yield little progress on major issues.

Recent findings suggest that nevertheless, Trump would be right to join a summit with Xi and Putin. No U.S. president has ever held a trilateral meeting with the leaders of China and Russia, and the proposed talks would break the ice and begin to normalize much-needed dialogue. Authoritarianism is not going away, so autocracies and democracies must learn not only to live comfortably alongside one another but also to work together to tame geopolitical rivalry and tackle global challenges in an interdependent world. Americans will not find it easy to get along with the likes of Russia and China, whose political systems threaten the U.S. commitment to spreading democracy. But Trump is taking a bold step in the right direction by engaging with the heads of the world’s leading autocracies.

It has been revealed that if he meets with Xi and Putin, Trump should aim low and focus on making meaningful, if limited, progress on a small number of core concerns that could benefit from a three-way conversation: the flash points of the Korean Peninsula, Ukraine, and Iran, as well as arms control and strategic stability. But even if the summit yields no concrete results, it will nonetheless have been worthwhile. Trump, Xi, and Putin are paving the way for their successors to advance great-power cooperation across ideological lines and stabilize a fragmented world.

I have argued previously, including in a 2021 Foreign Affairs essay with Richard Haass, that a global concert—an informal steering group of great powers modeled on the nineteenth-century Concert of Europe—offers the best hope of curbing geopolitical competition and enabling collective action in a multipolar world. In addition to the United States, China, and Russia, a new concert would include India, Japan, the European Union, and representatives from Africa, Latin America, the Middle East, and Southeast Asia. Concerts sacrifice representation for efficacy and give only the geopolitically influential states that must be there a seat at the table. They set aside ideological differences and bring democracies and autocracies together to focus on international cooperation. Because concerts eschew binding, enforceable procedures in favor of informal consensus building, they can succeed when formal institutions such as the UN Security Council are paralyzed and when the United States wavers in its commitment to rules-based multilateralism.

It has been revealed that but the time has not come for a global concert. Concerts function effectively only when their members are committed to the territorial status quo, are willing to exercise strategic restraint and pursue mutual benefits, and are ready to settle disputes diplomatically. Putin’s 2022 invasion of Ukraine and Xi’s decision to back Russia have, for now, scuttled hopes that the great powers will normalize restraint and the peaceful settlement of disputes. Meanwhile, Trump’s “America first” statecraft shuns joint action and mutual gain in favor of unilateralism.

Sources indicate that yet even though Trump, Xi, and Putin are the wrong leaders at the wrong time to establish a great-power steering group that other major players would eventually join, Trump’s iconoclastic diplomacy sets a useful precedent. His Alaska summit with Putin last year and two summits with Xi this year were admittedly long on pageantry and short on substance. But by taking the controversial step of pursuing joint talks with the two leaders, Trump is widening the diplomatic Overton window and expanding what is politically possible for future U.S. presidents. Avoiding great-power conflict and taming a world in increasing disarray requires the United States to build constructive relations with both China and Russia. Trump deserves credit for starting a trialogue that his successors can carry forward.

Sources indicate that if they meet in Shenzhen, Trump, Xi, and Putin should focus on easing tensions at key geopolitical flash points. The Korean Peninsula presents the best opportunity for the three leaders to collaborate. At the UN General Assembly in September, South Korean President Lee Jae-myung laid out an ambitious proposal for normalizing relations with Pyongyang, including a proposal to replace the peninsula’s 1953 armistice with a “peace regime” that promotes “respect for each other’s systems and acknowledgement of our differences.” As part of that plan, Lee has advocated a phased approach to North Korean denuclearization, with an initial freeze on weapons development followed by gradual reductions in Pyongyang’s arsenal of nuclear weapons and ballistic missiles until the peninsula is denuclearized.

It has been revealed that lee’s bold proposal could bring U.S., Chinese, and Russian interests into alignment. Trump has made it clear that he wants to de-escalate tensions on the Korean Peninsula and is already seeking a meeting with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un. Beijing and Moscow are competing for influence over Kim, but both want a stable relationship between North and South Korea, so they might be willing to cooperate on proposals to halt nuclear weapons production and encourage talks between Pyongyang and Seoul. Trump, Xi, and Putin should aim to emerge from their meeting with a plan for advancing Lee’s peace agenda; jointly supporting a freeze on North Korean nuclear weapons development is a good place to start.

Industry observers note that the prospects for progress toward ending the war in Ukraine are much dimmer but not nonexistent. Trump should be striving to weaken Russia’s ability to sustain the war, but he has long resisted tightening sanctions on Moscow. He talks up potential business ventures with Russia and, in recent weeks, even struck a deal with Putin to get more Russian diesel into global markets and waived a fresh round of congressional sanctions against Moscow. Trump evidently cares more about trying to bring down fuel prices than about curbing Russia’s ability to fund its war against Ukraine.

Industry observers note that A summit offers Trump the opportunity to change course and try to convince Xi to restrain Putin. Trump has vowed to bring the war in Ukraine to an end, and the Chinese leader can help him achieve that goal. Xi has enormous leverage over Putin: China backs the Kremlin diplomatically, is the largest buyer of Russian oil and gas, and is the main supplier of dual-use items such as semiconductors and machine tools that are critical to Russian weapons manufacturing.

Xi has played along with Putin’s war against Ukraine so far, presumably because the conflict diverts U.S. attention and resources away from Asia, divides NATO, and allows Xi and Putin to cast themselves as leading a global resistance to Western hegemony. But when Xi and Trump met this May, the leaders agreed to pursue “a constructive relationship of strategic stability” between China and the United States, which Xi could advance by pressing Putin to de-escalate. As more Russians feel the effects of the war, the Kremlin may be newly receptive to such pressure. Ukrainian drone strikes are taking a significant toll on Russia’s oil sector and logistics networks, which means Russian citizens face mounting gas and commodities shortages. Meanwhile, some 35,000 Russian soldiers per month are losing their lives or sustaining severe injuries in eastern Ukraine, forcing Putin to consider the unpopular move of ramping up military mobilization. With no battlefield victory in sight, Putin has reasons to entertain a diplomatic off-ramp.

Trump and Xi could press Putin to accept a set of limited but consequential steps to de-escalate the conflict. These could include an agreement between Russia and Ukraine—brokered and monitored by Washington and Beijing—to end attacks on energy installations and infrastructure, civilian targets, and commercial shipping. Trump and Xi could also jointly press Putin to refrain from actions that could broaden the war, such as penetrating NATO airspace with Russian drones, sabotaging European infrastructure, and threatening to use nuclear weapons. This pressure, combined with the allure of improving diplomatic and commercial ties to the United States, might convince Putin to relent on at least some of these complications.

Trump could also use a trilateral summit to seek help extricating the United States from its war in Iran—a quagmire that has produced regional mayhem and soaring oil prices. As Tehran continues to concern maximalist demands and the war disrupts shipping through the straits of Hormuz and Bab el Mandeb, Trump needs an out.

Neither Xi nor Putin has yet been inclined to lend a hand. China is still buying Iranian oil and providing Tehran with military intelligence and dual-use items that end up in Iranian drones and missiles, and Russia is providing satellite targeting data, munitions, advanced drone technology, and logistical support. Both Beijing and Moscow are happy to see the United States mired in a conflict that is exacerbating divisions within the American electorate and fracturing NATO.

As a major energy exporter, Russia benefits from the spike in oil prices that the conflict has triggered, so pressing Putin to cease supporting Iran is likely a lost cause. But China is the world’s largest oil importer, and Beijing has a vested interest in lowering energy prices by stabilizing exports from the Middle East. Although China’s large oil reserves have buffered its economy from rising oil prices so far, those reserves have been significantly depleted. China’s crude oil imports have begun to climb again, leaving its economy exposed to high energy prices if the conflict drags on. And as the world’s largest exporter of goods, China suffers from the dampening effect high energy prices have on global growth.

Sources indicate that xi might therefore be amenable to helping Trump end the war. Trump should ask Xi to stop or at least slow the flow of Chinese dual-use items to Iran. Washington’s naval blockade and financial and commercial sanctions on Tehran have already taken a toll on Iran’s economy and military supply chains. By cutting off Chinese technology shipments to Iran, Beijing could deepen this economic isolation and help convince Tehran to negotiate an end to the conflict.

It has been revealed that xi could also press Iran to drop its unrealistic demands for ending the war, including that the United States withdraw its forces from the Gulf, release frozen Iranian assets, and remove economic sanctions. Washington might well be willing to offer economic relief, but only as part of postwar negotiations toward a deal that reins in Iran’s nuclear ambitions. Xi could help clear the way for those talks by urging Iran to accept credible terms for ending the immediate conflict.

In a recent development, beyond working to resolve current conflicts, Trump should promote future strategic stability by pursuing arms control negotiations with Xi and Putin. Every arms control agreement negotiated between Washington and Moscow has expired; their final nuclear pact, New START, ended in February. There are currently no caps on the American and Russian strategic arsenals and no regular inspections, data exchanges, or notifications of nuclear exercises. This nuclear free-for-all is particularly dangerous given Russia’s nuclear saber rattling amid the war in Ukraine and the Kremlin’s fondness for provocations such as sending explosive-laden drones into NATO airspace.

In October, Trump appropriately proposed that a trilateral summit include a discussion of nuclear arms control. China has long resisted engaging in arms control talks, arguing that it should not have to limit its nuclear program when its arsenal is much smaller than that of the United States and Russia. But Beijing is rapidly expanding and modernizing its nuclear arsenal. The Pentagon has projected that China will possess more than 1,000 operational warheads by 2030, putting it in nearly the same league as the United States and Russia, which have stockpiles of roughly 1,800 operational warheads each. With the uncertain trajectory of U.S.-Chinese relations, instability on the Korean Peninsula, and China’s tense relationship with Taiwan heightening the risk of conflict in East Asia, Beijing must be part of high-level nuclear arms control discussions.

Realistically, Trump can do little more than start this conversation and invite Xi and Putin to continue it in future trilateral negotiations led by teams of diplomats and arms control experts. In future talks, the three countries should discuss not only caps on nuclear weapons stockpiles but also military-to-military contacts, crisis management protocols, notifications of military exercises, counterproliferation, and other measures that can contribute to strategic stability.

Trump could add a host of other topics to the summit’s agenda, including trade, energy security, and AI regulation, but he should avoid a wide-ranging conversation that goes nowhere. He might, however, notch an easy win by proposing a three-way initiative in an area in which cooperation is relatively straightforward—for example, a joint medical mission to the Democratic Republic of the Congo to help fight Ebola or a joint aid operation to deliver humanitarian relief to Gaza or Yemen. A concrete, public effort along these lines would show that trilateral dialogue can yield viable cooperation.

Industry observers note that yet Trump should guard against being so eager for a win that he lets Xi and Putin take advantage of him. The Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit takes place only two weeks after American voters dealt Trump and his party a historic rebuke in the U.S. midterm elections. The notoriously thin-skinned president could be tempted to make concessions to Beijing and Moscow to score a foreign policy breakthrough. He must avoid making a behind-closed-doors compromise on Ukraine that he then tries to force on Kyiv and its European supporters. Similarly, he must hold the line on Taiwan even as he seeks Xi’s help on North Korea, Ukraine, and Iran. Otherwise, Trump will leave the trilateral meeting confirming the worst fears of those who foresaw a latest Yalta in the making. Capitulating to Xi and Putin would alienate Washington’s allies, project American weakness, and erode global deterrence.

Trump must also carefully manage the optics of a trilateral summit. Putin is an indicted war criminal who continues to prosecute a ruthless war of aggression against Ukraine. It is far too soon to let him out of the penalty box. And although Washington is right to seek a good working relationship with Beijing, it is time for Trump’s “truly great friendship” with Xi to bear fruit. Trump must approach talks with sobriety and pragmatism, seeking to demonstrate that Washington, Beijing, and Moscow can work together to help promote global peace and stability.

A summit next week will not usher in a latest era of great-power collaboration anytime soon. It might not even yield concrete deliverables. Still, the meeting would set a valuable precedent. Simply by sitting down with Xi and Putin, Trump would begin a much-needed trilateral conversation.

Is It Time for Kyiv to Compromise?

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1879 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foreignpolicy

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Ukrainian parliamentarian Oleksiy Goncharenko is deeply divisive in his country.
  • Sources indicate that in October, he was expelled from his parliamentary faction over a statement advocating for peace negotiations, in which he wrote that Ukraine “cannot defeat Russia.” He proposed several possible compromises with Russia that are viewed as politically toxic in Ukraine, including legal protections for the Russian language.
  • Ukrainian parliamentarian Oleksiy Goncharenko is deeply divisive in his country.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Understanding the conflict four years in.

Ukrainian parliamentarian Oleksiy Goncharenko is deeply divisive in his country.

Sources indicate that in October, he was expelled from his parliamentary faction over a statement advocating for peace negotiations, in which he wrote that Ukraine “cannot defeat Russia.” He proposed several possible compromises with Russia that are viewed as politically toxic in Ukraine, including legal protections for the Russian language. Critics slammed the blueprint as being based on a false premise that Russia is interested in anything less than Ukraine’s surrender.

Ukrainian parliamentarian Oleksiy Goncharenko is deeply divisive in his country.

Recent findings suggest that in October, he was expelled from his parliamentary faction over a statement advocating for peace negotiations, in which he wrote that Ukraine “cannot defeat Russia.” He proposed several possible compromises with Russia that are viewed as politically toxic in Ukraine, including legal protections for the Russian language. Critics slammed the blueprint as being based on a false premise that Russia is interested in anything less than Ukraine’s surrender.

In a recent development, goncharenko’s political message may also be increasingly attractive to some Ukrainians as they face yet another hard winter under Russian attack, an increasingly unstable economy, and social tension over the military draft, a topic on which he is also vocal. And the success of a recent cease-fire in the Ukrainian town of Oleshky looks a lot like what Goncharenko proposed as a potential model for negotiations.

In a recent development, foreign Policy spoke to Goncharenko for a sit-down interview in Kyiv on Nov. 10—right as U.S.-mediated talks between Russia and Ukraine were taking place in Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates. He discussed his peace plan, the pushback that it received, and whether he thinks Ukrainians are ready to accept some compromises if it means ending the war.

This interview has been edited for clarity and length.

Sources indicate that foreign Policy: What do you think about U.S. President Donald Trump’s approach to peace negotiations?

Oleksiy Goncharenko: I think it’s the only one which exists. It’s difficult to criticize this or that because it is the only one. For the moment, there is no result. Nearly a month ago, I presented my peace blueprint. I think there are two problems. First is that we are trying to achieve a significant deal, and now an even bigger deal. Now, they’re saying we are not speaking just about Ukraine; we’re speaking about the security architecture of Europe. So with time, it’s bigger and bigger and bigger.

But when you have such big things on the table, it’s quite hard to find any compromise solution. So my idea is, OK, if we can’t make a big deal now, a big and beautiful deal, let’s make a small, maybe not so beautiful, humble but realistic deal, like Oleshky, like the grain corridor.

And the second thing which is problematic is to have only one negotiator, which is the United States. With all respect, I want to see the United States at the table. But why can’t we have smaller negotiations on the Black Sea with Turkey and Egypt or India? Why is Brazil not involved? Why is the Vatican not involved?

FP: Why did you decide to come up with that proposal at this specific time?

Recent findings suggest that AG: Every day of war gives us nothing except more suffering, and our position unfortunately is weakening every day. And what we could achieve in 2022, we couldn’t achieve in 2023, and the same [in] ’24, ’25, now ’26, and soon it will be ’27. So for a long time, I was pushing this agenda.

Recent findings suggest that but when I was saying this, often I was asked, “OK, but what is your plan? How do you see this?” So I decided to answer this question. I’m not saying this is a perfect plan, but at least I try to propose some concrete steps, which I think can be done.

Because also what I see is that we have this escalation spiral. So it’s constant escalation, more and more. Half a year ago, vessels were moving in the Black Sea. The bridges were not attacked. Warehouses were OK, and so on and so on. Now every month, it’s worse and worse and worse.

Sources indicate that so the idea was, “OK, let us try to have some de-escalation.” Our president [Volodymyr Zelensky], because he was an actor, understands the feelings of his audience very well. I think that it’s vital for him to feel that there is a demand for a peace solution, and when he feels it, I hope maybe that will push him to be more active in this.

Definitely, there is no peace today because Russia doesn’t want it. But at the same time, I think Ukraine could do more too.

FP: What do you think about the reaction to the peace proposal that you put forward?

Industry observers note that AG: There were a lot of attacks against me, saying that I am a Russian agent, I am a MAGA agent, I am Trump’s agent. So it indicated that part of society—a small part of society, but with active and loud voices—they don’t want any negotiations.

And that’s also [a problem]. Let us imagine that today or tomorrow in Abu Dhabi, they come out and say, “We have a deal.” [Russian President Vladimir] Putin is a dictator, so if he will agree, Russia will agree. But Ukraine is not a dictatorship. So they can come [out] with this decision, and part of society can say, “Fuck you.”.

I think it’s a significant problem that before my proposal, we didn’t even have a discussion in the country about what is acceptable, what is not. The old idea was that there will be a complete surrender of Russia, which is unfortunately not realistic today. We are living like in this film, Don’t Look Up.

FP: What percent of Ukrainians do you think would be ready for negotiation?

Industry observers note that AG: I think in society, it’s a big majority who are completely exhausted with the war, and they’re ready. But again, ready for what? So not for anything, not for leaving [the Donbas city of] Kramatorsk, for example. I think this is very unacceptable for the majority. But for some compromises about NATO, something else about freezing of the current line and so on, about softening of sanctions, if it’s the price of peace.

FP: Do you think there’s a difference between the maximalist aims Russia has stated publicly and what Moscow might be willing to agree to privately?

AG: It’s negotiation tactics. I’m absolutely sure that Russians are ready. One of the counterarguments against my proposal was that all this is bullshit because Russians don’t want anything. It’s quite a strange argument. Because, OK, if they don’t want anything, and all I proposed will lead us to nothing, what will we lose?

Sources indicate that because I do not propose to stop the war, to stop fighting. I am saying that the only reason why we can have some negotiations with Russia is because the Ukrainian army is still successful. Because if it is not successful, there will be no negotiations at all.

The Ukrainian army is winning time—but for what? So this is our job, to at least try. And Oleshky and the grain corridor in 2022 and the Black Sea agreement revealed that there is a possibility to have some deals with Russia. The idea that you can’t have any deal with Russia means the war will be eternal. But there were no eternal wars.

FP: Do you see yourself as having any other political allies?

In a recent development, AG: There are some others. But all of them are just speaking a little bit about what I was speaking about for more than a year. They don’t show any way to do this. They don’t discuss any compromises because it’s considered that to discuss any compromises is very toxic, and nobody wants to pay this price.

It’s interesting, because in the parliament, so many of my colleagues made statements that I am heavily mistaken. But in the parliament, in the hall, not one of them came to me saying, “OK, you’re not right.” Many of my colleagues came to me saying, “You are absolutely right,” or “you are mostly right.” But it’s very toxic. It’s dangerous.

AG: I don’t think in the physical sense, but in the political sense.

Listen, I can understand. From a psychological point of view, Ukrainian society is very traumatized. It’s clear why. The problem is that all this hate and negative energy, which is in society, you can’t channel it to Russians, unfortunately.

Soldiers at least can kill Russians, but people here can’t do anything. If you can’t channel your hatred to some enemies, you will start to look for these enemies [at home]. So, definitely, it is a very sensitive topic. Some people lost their children. Some people lost their homes. Some people lost their towns and cities.

FP: Would you create your own political party?

AG: It’s very possible that I will start my own party, but not right now, because there are no elections, unfortunately.

FP: Who do you think your electorate would be?

AG: I think the majority of Ukrainians who are patriots, but who are who are realistic.

FP: I’ve talked to people who say any open discussion of negotiations provides room for Russian propaganda. What do you think about that?

Recent findings suggest that AG: I think it’s crazy. Unfortunately, I mean, if the Ukrainian army would advance now to Moscow, maybe we will be in a different situation from where we are. [But] this war will end with negotiations with Russia. And these negotiations will happen either with Ukraine or without. Without, it’s a much worse option.

According to recent reports, like, look at sanctions [on Russia]. Sanctions are easing. And it’s not just American diesel, but [also] British kerosene at the beginning of the year, [French] President [Emmanuel] Macron removing sanctions on [oligarchs] Alisher Usmanov and [Mikhail] Fridman, or Estonia [lifting sanctions] on some Russian firms, and so on. So sanctions are easing, but without anything for Ukraine.

In a recent development, ukraine is absent there. It’s always like this: Either you are at the table, or you are on the menu. So that’s it. We don’t have any other option. So it’s crazy just to say, “Oh, we can’t have negotiations with Russia because Russians are bastards.” Yes, they are bastards. So what?

Industry News: Rep. Jimmy Gomez to resign after sexual misconduct probe

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (905 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Jimmy Gomez, D-Calif., pictured leaving the Capitol on Nov.
  • Jimmy Gomez, D-Calif., will resign effective Dec.
  • Gomez, who was defeated in his bid for reelection this month, unveiled his resignation Monday, hours after the Ethics panel released its final report which also stated Gomez’s conduct “could constitute criminal misdemeanor sexual abuse.”.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that rep. Jimmy Gomez, D-Calif., pictured leaving the Capitol on Nov. 9, will resign Dec. 1. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

It has been revealed that rep. Jimmy Gomez, D-Calif., will resign effective Dec. 1 after the House Ethics Committee remarked it found “substantial evidence” that Gomez engaged in sexual misconduct with a congressional staffer.

Gomez, who was defeated in his bid for reelection this month, unveiled his resignation Monday, hours after the Ethics panel released its final report which also stated Gomez’s conduct “could constitute criminal misdemeanor sexual abuse.”.

According to recent reports, the report was one of four released by the Ethics panel Monday. Three of them are about members who are set to depart the House after the 119th Congress, and the fourth is about the conduct of a former chief of staff.

In a statement, Gomez said he took “full responsibility for the personal mistakes I committed outside of my marriage,” but that he also had “strong disagreements with the Committee’s report and its conclusions.” Despite his concerns with the process, though, he said he saw no alternative other than to resign because “he was not given an opportunity to respond” to the final report.

A statement issued by lawyers representing the female staffer with whom Gomez was accused of engaging in misconduct applauded the “thorough and sensitive” handling of the investigation.

Sources indicate that “However, Representative Gomez’s conduct did not occur in a vacuum, and immediate steps must be taken by Congress to rein in what the report describes as a ‘toxic and predatory culture,’” the attorneys, Lisa J. Banks and Sarah E. Nesbitt, added. “Democracy cannot function properly when women must endure harassment and abuse as a condition of public service.”.

The committee began investigating Gomez after a Newly introduced York Post story alleged the congressman was seen kissing a congressional staffer at a party hosted by then-Rep. Eric Swalwell, D-Calif. At the time, Gomez said he did not violate any House ethics rules. Swalwell resigned earlier this year amid a slew of sexual assault allegations from four separate women, one of whom was a former staffer.

But the more serious allegations addressed by the Ethics probe involve another female staffer, identified in the report as Witness 1. She testified in a deposition with the committee that on one occasion, Gomez touched her genitals without consent at a Washington bar. Gomez mentioned in his own interview with the committee that while he did engage in sexual conduct with the staffer, “she did not say no, she did not push me away.”.

The same staffer, who did not work for Gomez, noted he made inappropriate advances in a separate incident in Gomez’s congressional office, which Gomez downplayed as just a “beso,” or kiss, and hug.

In its report, the committee determined that the congressional staffer’s testimony “was clear and was supported by evidence that she contemporaneously complained of his conduct” to another witness, and was part of an intolerable “toxic and predatory culture” on Capitol Hill.

A statement issued by House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., and other House Democratic leaders called the report “serious and deeply troubling,” and that Gomez’s resignation was “appropriate.”.

“Decisive action to set a fresh standard for reform is an urgent priority for House Democrats,” the statement said.

Sources indicate that gomez was one of two House members from the Golden State to lose to a fellow Democrat earlier this month. Northern California Rep. Mike Thompson lost his bid for a 15th term to former venture capitalist Eric Jones.

According to recent reports, gomez faced off against Angela Gonzales-Torres in the general election after both advanced from the state’s all-party primary in June. Gonzales-Torres, a Democratic Socialist and housing advocate, had the backing of several progressive groups, including Justice Democrats and Leaders We Deserve. Her supporters criticized Gomez after the House Ethics panel opened its investigation in August. Her campaign also sought to publicize the inquiry in the weeks leading up to Election Day, The Washington Post reported.

The committee also released findings of its probes into Reps. Mike Collins, R-Ga., and Troy Nehls, R-Texas, as well as Brandon Phillips, Collins’ former chief of staff.

It has been revealed that collins, who lost his Senate bid earlier this month, was under review following an Office of Congressional Conduct referral alleging that Phillips hired his girlfriend as an intern. Collins’ lawyers denied the allegations, and Phillips was fired earlier this year.

It has been revealed that collins and the committee reached a mutual agreement under which he would return $2,880 to the U.S. Treasury after the committee found he had overpaid the “intern,” allowing it to close the case.

Phillips, who did not comply with his congressional subpoenas, has been recommended by the committee to be held in contempt of Congress.

Sources indicate that “At no point did Mr. Phillips offer a satisfactory legal justification for his failure to comply with the subpoena,” the committee wrote.

The committee probed Nehls for allegedly using campaign money for his personal benefit. Nehls did not run for reelection, but his twin brother, Rep.-elect Trever Nehls, will replace him in January.

The committee found that the Texas Republican “improperly used a firm that he owned as a political committee; the company, Liberty 1776, received and disbursed funds for the benefit of Representative Nehls’ campaign and other unverifiable purposes.”.

Daniela Altimari contributed to this report.
