📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that democrat Victoria Broderick, seen here speaking to a reporter outside the Capitol on Nov. 11, has unseated Republican Rep. Scott DesJarlais in Tennessee's 4th District. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call) (Bill Clark CQ Roll Call).

It has been revealed that democrat Victoria Broderick has defeated Republican Rep. Scott DesJarlais in Tennessee’s 4th District, giving her party the 259th seat of its commanding House majority in the next Congress.

Broderick, a tech support worker, was leading by 361 votes when The Associated Press called the race Tuesday, three weeks after all votes were cast.

Broderick’s victory ranks among the most surprising Democratic wins of this year’s midterm elections. DesJarlais, who defeated Broderick in 2024 by more than 40 points, was not considered vulnerable heading into Election Day.

But the election two years ago took place under a previous version of Tennessee’s congressional map. Following this spring’s Supreme Court ruling that limited the use of race in redistricting, the state’s Republican-led legislature redrew the House lines to eliminate Rep. Steve Cohen’s Memphis-area district, the lone seat held by Democrats.

In doing so, though, the new map significantly altered the boundaries of the largely rural 4th District in Middle Tennessee, which now extends into Nashville’s Davidson County. Thirty-three percent of DesJarlais’ constituents were new to him, according to calculations by Inside Elections with Nathan L. Gonzales, as the district shifted from one that Donald Trump carried by 43 points in 2024 to one that would have backed him by 24 points.

Under the upcoming map, Republicans struggled to win most of the state’s House seats earlier this month. They narrowly won Cohen’s 9th District, one of just three flips for the party this year nationwide. But Broderick’s win ensures that Tennessee will continue to have a Democrat in its congressional delegation.

DesJarlais had already conceded the race before Tuesday’s AP call.

Industry observers note that “As the final votes have now been tabulated in this fresh and completely restructured district, it appears that we have a result showing my campaign has come just a few hundred votes short out of just under 200,000 votes cast,” he remarked in a Nov. 16 statement congratulating Broderick.

A member of the hard-line conservative Freedom Caucus, DesJarlais was first elected in 2010, unseating Democrat Lincoln Davis. While he’d been comfortably reelected in the years since, he faced competitive primaries in 2014 and 2016 after his divorce records came to light.

In a recent development, broderick, a mother of two and a former chair of the Lincoln County Democratic Party, raised less than $100,000 for her campaign, compared with more than $650,000 for DesJarlais. She also defeated a better-funded opponent in the Democratic primary.

She told PBS NewsHour that she had essentially been campaigning for the seat since launching her 2024 bid and built relationships across the district that helped her win.

It has been revealed that “I never stopped running for Congress. And when it was redistricted, I just essentially noted, well, the district stayed the same and actually became more competitive,” she said. “So the work's going to start speaking for itself real soon. And we saw that happen.”.

According to recent reports, three House races remain uncalled as of Tuesday afternoon. Louisiana will hold runoffs in December for two districts, including a Democrat-held seat that Republicans redrew in their favor. The race for Minnesota’s 1st District is heading for a hand recount, with Republican Rep. Brad Finstad trailing Democratic challenger Jake Johnson by 324 votes.

Put out of mind the scenes of cheering you may have seen of Jensen Huang’s return to the headquarters of perhaps the world’s most key manufacturer, Nvidia, marking his personally triumphant comeback from being unanimously ousted by his board.

Recent findings suggest that get out of your thoughts any happy notions that you have reason to celebrate just because your money, like the money of so many millions of Americans and people well beyond the country’s borders, is tied up in the U.S. stock market, which soared at this surprising turn in the news after slumping badly in response to the scandals that had swirled around Huang.

Put out of mind the scenes of cheering you may have seen of Jensen Huang’s return to the headquarters of perhaps the world’s most crucial tech giant, Nvidia, marking his personally triumphant comeback from being unanimously ousted by his board.

Get out of your thoughts any happy notions that you have reason to celebrate just because your money, like the money of so many millions of Americans and people well beyond the country’s borders, is tied up in the U.S. stock market, which soared at this surprising turn in the news after slumping badly in response to the scandals that had swirled around Huang.

Recent findings suggest that what has happened in recent days, culminating in Huang’s return in the face of allegations he sustained a secret affair with a woman who was in touch with China’s spy agencies, is bad news for an economy that has grown increasingly imbalanced with the enormous growth of artificial intelligence. Far better for the U.S. economy and for everyone who has a stake in it would have been a reckoning for Nvidia that forced it to undertake the hard work of corporate reform and rebuilding trust.

Sources indicate that nvidia, for those who have not been paying attention, makes the most indispensable product in the world of AI: graphics processing units, a specialized type of chip, so capable and advanced that it has few real competitors, including, crucially, among well-funded Chinese companies. Nvidia, however, is much more than even this. As I have written before, it sits at the center of a highly incestuous economy of AI companies, including most of the significant service providers, which it funds to keep purchasing its chips. The circular funding arrangements that Nvidia sustains with its largest customers—companies with extraordinary financial leverage and seemingly bottomless capital needs—is what keeps the AI economy’s party going. Without this, the merry-go-round of this latest sector would grind to a halt and make what many thought looked like a bursting bubble in recent days seem like a minor blip.

Recent findings suggest that add to this the fact that the U.S. government and President Donald Trump have seemingly become convinced that everything and anything must be permitted with Nvidia, and with AI in general, or else China will overtake the United States in the most key technology of the near future. What this gives you is something more frightening than too massive to fail: a tech giant declared too strategically important to question or to hold to account.

In a recent development, the reality is that almost everything about the present picture is messed up and deeply worrisome. Let’s start with the fact that Trump, who already leads a government largely unconstrained by Congress and with wildly inflated executive powers, has taken so freely to intervening in the running of major companies. In Huang’s case, he played a central role in his reinstatement, as Monday’s news revealed.

Sources indicate that there is nothing reassuring about this, but it gets worse. There is no reason to believe that Trump has an even remotely sophisticated grasp of the technologies at the heart of Nvidia’s business or its race against competitors. What we do know is that Trump has a weakness for very powerful and wealthy men, and Huang fits this billing. In the president’s universe, he is a winner, and Trump loves to associate himself with anyone invested with such an aura. Trump even posted an AI-generated photo of Huang intended to mirror a famous image of himself after surviving an assassination attempt, with the big difference that Huang was shown hoisting a red bra.

Trump, furthermore, is not known for a deep concern about ethics, and that is putting things gently. Where do ethics enter into this? Everywhere, from Huang’s honesty and the extent to which he was forthcoming about his affair with the suspicious Chinese national and shadowy customer, Alice Huang, as well as with at least one other woman who was his direct subordinate at Nvidia, in violation of corporate rules. Ethics are also involved in the way Huang ran his manufacturer, with a historically supine board, minimal internal controls on his behavior and oversight, and the way he promoted his family members. What matters is that nothing, inside the company or outside it, checked him. In fact, it seems likely that Trump, with his own record of serial marriages, rumored affairs, and children on the make, can relate.

Recent findings suggest that but even these are mere starters. If competition with China deserves inclusion in any serious conversation about the future of AI, Trump’s treatment of Huang’s situation at Nvidia has been a running chronicle of flagrant disregard for national security. Let’s count the ways. First, when the U.S. government began to look into Alice Huang’s behavior on the suspicion that she might be a spy, it never informed Jensen Huang or gave him what would have been typical: a so-called defensive briefing so that he would know what to look out for and avoid giving away valuable trade secrets or selling his firm’s most advanced chips without adequate controls preventing them from being shipped onward to China.

Recent findings suggest that more broadly, historians may come to see Trump’s casual disregard for normal considerations of national security to be one of the most key and unusual hallmarks of his time in power. The examples are numerous. When shown evidence that Russia or China or some other powerful adversary is conducting secret operations against U.S. interests, Trump has often waved away concerns—in effect saying, well, we do that to them, too.

In a recent development, last week offered the spectacle of Trump mugging in China with that country’s leader and Russia’s Vladimir Putin, with no hint that he had complained to them about offering targeting information to Iran that has enabled that country to attack U.S. bases in the Middle East, killing U.S. troops, as is the case with Russia, or supplying drone components to Iran, as with China. Trump went yet further, though, looking like a kid in a candy shop as he entered a room to greet an awaiting Putin and exclaiming, “He’s my friend.” Lest the message be lost on anyone, he later posted a picture of the meeting with this same message on social media.

Second, there is further reason to distrust the judgment of the U.S. government in the unfolding Nvidia saga. It lies in the vague and unforthcoming way its officials have spoken about Huang and his erstwhile Chinese mistress since their affair became public knowledge, always carefully avoiding clarity about whether or not she might have been a spy or whether his behavior damaged U.S. national security interests.

In fairness, the question of whether she was a spy involves some nuance. Alice Huang could very well have compromised U.S. national security without being a member or agent of any Chinese intelligence service in a formal sense. The lack of openness and straight language about the other question leaves little wiggle room, though. Through the Singapore-based manufacturer she worked for, Alice Huang was purchasing Nvidia’s most advanced chips, which fall under explicit U.S. export controls to China. This puts the public in a bewildering place. On the one hand, people are asked to believe that the United States must beat China in a zero-sum race toward the AI future. On the other, given the lack of candor about these Nvidia sales and the damage they may have caused to U.S. interests, we are being told, in effect, one of Trump’s favorite messages: Smile, and be happy. Lots of money was being made.

Taken together, Nvidia and Jensen Huang seem to concentrate enormous and growing risk for the entire public, as does the broader AI sector. Remember that Anthropic, the leading AI provider that went public recently, has warned of the potential power of its systems becoming so awesome as to having the potential to lead us all to an extinction-level event. And when the world’s top AI power is led by someone with such a casual disregard for safeguards, for strong governance, for ethics and for transparency, a company too crucial to question invites a peril that risks falling on us all.

It has been revealed that newly unsealed search warrant documents reveal a decades-long federal investigation into Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., going back to 1980. Former federal prosecutor Jonathan Fahey joins 'Fox & Friends' to analyze the records and the Department of Justice's search for evidence of redacted crimes. Fahey discusses the legal implications of the unsealed warrant for her Washington, D.C. home.

Court documents released Monday night showed U.S. Department of Justice prosecutors battling with U.S. Magistrate Judge Matthew J. Sharbaugh to obtain a search warrant for the Washington, D.C., home of Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn.

The DOJ applied to the magistrate for a search warrant on Oct. 2, eventually receiving the warrant which led to a Homeland Security Investigations search of the home on Oct. 12.

However, the newly released petition for the warrant reveals the court raised concerns that the DOJ could be violating the Constitution’s Speech and Debate Clause.

FEDERAL AGENTS RAID ILHAN OMAR’S DC HOME AMID IMMIGRATION FRAUD INVESTIGATION.

It has been revealed that "The search warrant here is directed to a sitting member of the United States House of Representatives. This means that, even after ensuring that there exists probable cause to issue the warrant, see Fed. R. Crim. P. 41(d)(1), the Court must separately balance any necessary constitutional considerations under governing precedent," the court wrote in a memorandum.

Is China Misreading the Moment?

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 16 min read (3251 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foreignaffairs

⏱️ ~16 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that RUSH DOSHI is an Assistant Professor at Georgetown University and Director of the China Strategy Initiative at the Council on Foreign Relations.
  • Beijing’s Overreach Threatens the Détente With America.
  • President Donald Trump lands in Shenzhen later this week for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit, he will sit down with Chinese leader Xi Jinping for the fourth time amid an unexpected détente between Washington and Beijing.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that RUSH DOSHI is an Assistant Professor at Georgetown University and Director of the China Strategy Initiative at the Council on Foreign Relations. He served as Director and Deputy Senior Director for China and Taiwan Affairs at the National Security Council from 2021 to 2024.

Beijing’s Overreach Threatens the Détente With America.

When U.S. President Donald Trump lands in Shenzhen later this week for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit, he will sit down with Chinese leader Xi Jinping for the fourth time amid an unexpected détente between Washington and Beijing. The trade war of 2025 is in abeyance, the two governments have revealed a relationship of “constructive strategic stability,” and, to the alarm of American allies, Trump and Xi are planning to meet with Russian President Vladimir Putin. Beneath the surface, however, the détente is beginning to crack.

Sources indicate that the relationship between Washington and Beijing looks remarkably different from the way it did a little over a year ago, when the two sides agreed to a truce in Busan, South Korea. In April 2025, Washington initiated the trade war by raising tariffs on China past 140 percent, and Beijing responded by restricting rare-earth exports later that month and threatening another cutoff that October. After Trump promptly backed down, the two leaders reached the deal in Busan: Washington would cap tariffs and suspend a specific export control regulation known as the Affiliates Rule in exchange for Beijing’s suspension of newly introduced export controls on minerals and magnets and the resumption of their normal flow to the United States. On that basis, both sides pursued a broad deescalation.

Industry observers note that since then, the Trump administration has been notably accommodating. Washington has kept new tariffs at 12.5 percent, well below the 20-percent ceiling Beijing previously agreed to. It has let advanced AI chips flow to China and to Chinese cutouts in Southeast Asia and has not added a Chinese firm to the Entity List in over the year, the longest pause since 2008. It has withheld arms sales from and downgraded defense talks with Taiwan, cut back naval transits of the Taiwan Strait, and raised doubts about U.S. support in the event of a crisis. And it has offered only muted support to such allies as Japan and the Philippines in the face of escalating Chinese coercion. All the while, Trump has praised Xi as a “great leader” and extended rare courtesies, including by welcoming Xi on the tarmac when he arrived in Washington for a state visit in September, the first such greeting of a foreign leader in 60 years.

Recent findings suggest that beijing has appreciated this accommodating approach—and seized the opportunity to act more assertively. It has viewed the competitive pause as temporary, a product of China’s growing strength and Trump’s admiration for Xi, and as a way to buy time to build advantage before the next eruption of tensions. With Washington occupied by its war in Iran and humbled by defeat in the last round of the trade war, Beijing has throttled the supply of minerals and magnets to the United States, taken steps to ensure that its industrial and technological gains remain in China, and increased pressure on its neighbors.

So far, Beijing has used the time well, advancing its objectives with little serious pushback from Washington. But China risks overreaching in its relationship with the United States. Not only is an incoming Democratic Congress likely to constrain Trump’s conciliatory China policy. There are also growing frustrations over Beijing’s unwillingness to fulfill the terms agreed to in Busan. Pressure on AI chips and export controls are emerging in the wake of revelations about the Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang’s relationship with an alleged Chinese spy and his company’s influence over U.S. export control policy. And new U.S. policies in response to the scandal could provoke a response from Beijing.

Recent findings suggest that xi and Trump will meet in Shenzhen and again in December in Miami, but with the January expiration of the Busan agreement looming in the background (and with no summits planned for next year), time is running out for the two leaders to extend and strengthen the current truce. If the détente falls apart the next time Washington’s and Beijing’s interests clash, China will be better prepared. It may also, perhaps hubristically, be more willing to escalate.

It has been revealed that although China favors Washington’s current accommodating approach and hopes it will last as long as possible, Beijing is also confident that it is strengthening its hand for a more contentious future. For China’s leaders, the current détente has been less an end goal than a temporary intermission, a means to build leverage ahead of the next round of strategic competition and, ultimately, a decisive long-term advantage.

Prominent Chinese scholars see the calm that followed Busan as tactical rather than strategic. Chen Dongxiao, the president of the Shanghai Institutes for International Studies, told the Shanghai news outlet The Paper that the two countries remain in a “tactical truce.” In May, Wu Xinbo of Fudan University told Beijing News, “If we can achieve a relationship of constructive strategic stability over the next three years, it will extend China’s period of strategic stability and win us time and space for development.” Writing in the journal International Review in August, he declared that the current “tactical stability” was “neither sustainable nor solid.” Shen Weizhong, a former Chinese foreign ministry official, was more blunt: “The more time we have, the better prepared we might be towards a final showdown on Taiwan or maybe another trade war.”.

In a recent development, beijing attributes little of the stabilization to Washington. In his August essay, Wu wrote that it “is not the result of the U.S. side having a change of heart or showing goodwill, but was won by China through arduous striving and struggle.” The United States had no choice; it simply needed the “breathing room.” Wang Yong, the director of Peking University’s American Studies Center, described the trade war as “a tipping point in terms of strength.” The former editor of the Global Times, Hu Xijin, wrote in a Weibo post after the U.S. midterm elections that “the current equilibrium in U.S.-China relations is the result of a contest of strength.” As Wu told The Paper in September, Washington has come to understand that Beijing “needs to be treated equally and with respect” and that China is “bolder about ‘drawing its sword.’” Keeping the supply of rare-earth minerals and magnets tight, to Beijing’s mind, might reinforce the current competitive pause rather than undermine it by reminding American leaders of China’s leverage.

It has been revealed that another critical factor in the current de-escalation, Chinese analysts argue, is Trump’s personality. Trump’s “distinct and unique decision-making style,” as Chen put it, has single-handedly blunted the more forceful defense of U.S. interests that members of his own administration and legislators in both parties favor. “He is often not entirely swayed by bipartisan opposition and still continues to pursue policies based on his own judgment,” Chen explained in the same interview. Writing in the Singaporean paper Lianhe Zaobao in September, Zhao Minghao of Fudan University more pointedly explained that Trump “admires power and prefers to engage with the leaders of powerful countries,” a stabilizing trait that benefits Beijing’s diplomacy while leaving allies and partners on the sidelines. “Of all modern U.S. presidents, Trump has cared the least about Taiwan,” one Guizhou-based commentator wrote. “He would readily sacrifice the island for his own interests.” An article reposted on the website of Qiushi, the Chinese Communist Party’s flagship journal, dwelt on Trump’s decision to greet Xi at the airport when he arrived for his state visit in September. The gesture, it claimed, “reflects the latest historical position of China-U.S. relations.”.

Sources indicate that but China also worries that Trump’s influence will decline over the next two years and perhaps cease altogether after 2028. Wang Hao, a professor at Fudan University’s Center for American Studies, told Phoenix News that the Democratic Party’s approach will not be “as pragmatic and flexible as the Trump administration’s,” a sentiment echoed across Chinese social media after the Democrats’ victory in the midterm elections.

The awareness that Trump’s approach may not survive beyond his presidency is precisely why Beijing has sought to lock it in through diplomacy. According to the Chinese readout, at the summit in May 2026, Xi declared that the relationship of “constructive strategic stability” he and Trump had agreed to build would provide guidance for U.S.-Chinese relations “over the next three years and beyond.” That duration was not accidental. As the scholar Zheng Yongnian put it at the time, the three-year window was “tailor-made for President Trump,” matching his current term. Beijing hopes it will bind his successor.

If diplomacy fails to secure U.S. deescalation, China hopes leverage will succeed. Over the last year, Beijing has used the time and space created by the détente to strengthen its position in industrial and technological competition with the United States. Beijing has long sought to make the world more dependent on China while reducing its own dependence on the world. But over the last year, that approach has evolved. Beijing has unveiled a raft of measures intended to ensure that its industrial, technological, and scientific know-how do not diffuse beyond China’s borders in order to lock in the country’s advantages.

Sources indicate that to keep foreign firms in China and blunt Western countries’ leverage over the Chinese economy, the State Council issued Orders 834 and 835, which effectively threaten companies that cut ties with Chinese partners or seek to exit the country with the risk of investigation, exclusion from the Chinese market, exit bans on executives, and possible criminal prosecution. To keep talent in China, Beijing has authorized exit bans on citizens considered possible risks to industrial or technological security and, according to Bloomberg, now requires travel approval for top AI and chip specialists and their families. And to keep scientific discoveries in China, the Ministry of State Security has warned researchers that they must clear security reviews before submitting articles to foreign journals. China has also imposed or proposed new export controls on dozens of technologies, from mining and batteries to AI models and biotechnology in order to protect its industrial capabilities. Beijing has even worked to prevent the transfer of equipment and engineers to India and Southeast Asia, stalled battery ventures with Indian firms, undermined Apple’s effort to move manufacturing to India, and issued a sweeping regulation that subjects Chinese investment abroad to a national security review more expansive than the United States’ own outbound investment review.

Beijing’s rare-earth licensing regime exemplifies China’s leverage-building strategy. To obtain a license, foreign buyers must hand over customer lists, the identities of their end users, and images of their production lines, all of which gives China insight into Western dependencies and helps it uncover chokepoints it can squeeze. Beijing has threatened to use these powers against countries that seek to protect themselves from the flood of Chinese manufactured goods entering their markets. In July, Beijing showed how precise it can now be in applying pressure when it cut off 14 European firms, including the German arms maker Rheinmetall, from Chinese dual-use exports in retaliation for EU sanctions related to Chinese support of Russia’s invasion of Ukraine.

Recent findings suggest that beijing has paired these measures at home with escalating pressure campaigns in its near abroad, betting that a distracted and chastened Washington will not come to the aid of China’s neighbors. That campaign has been most brazen in the South China Sea, where China has engaged in escalations unseen before the détente. Since Busan, Beijing has essentially abrogated its 2024 understanding with the Philippines, which maintained stability on the question of Second Thomas Shoal. In July, a Chinese coast guard boat rammed a Philippine navy inflatable and its crew clubbed a sailor on the head with a wooden baton, the most violent assault on Philippine personnel in years.

Industry observers note that the timing of these incidents has been provocative. In July, when Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi and U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio were in Manila for the Association of Southeast Asian Nations meetings, the coast guard released water-cannon attacks on Philippine vessels near Scarborough Shoal. Then, in September, during Xi’s U.S. state visit, Chinese warships and cutters blocked a Philippine resupply mission outright for the first time in two years. In October, Chinese cutters interfered with a medical evacuation from Second Thomas Shoal, delaying a patient transfer by ten hours. Last month, Beijing’s ambassador in Manila mused that if China chose to use force against the Philippines, “we may easily win.”.

In a recent development, china has also run its broadest coercion campaign against Japan in more than a decade, nominally in response to comments made by Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi on Taiwan. It has included a travel advisory, a seafood ban, a dual-use export ban, and curbs on rare-earth exports that have forced Japanese companies to contemplate shutting down operations. Chinese carrier-based fighters have locked their weapons-targeting radar onto Japanese jets. Beijing has also pursued newly introduced gas structures in the East China Sea and set a record 357-day coast guard presence in 2025 around the Japanese-administered Senkaku Islands (known in China as the Diaoyu Islands), with cutters now chasing Japanese fishing boats into territorial waters. Washington’s support for Tokyo has, so far, been limited.

Industry observers note that and around Taiwan, China has made its pressure quieter but more routine. In December 2025, during the People’s Liberation Army’s Justice Mission exercises, China fired live rockets closer to Taiwan than ever before, landing ten of them inside the island’s 24-nautical-mile contiguous zone. As of this summer, Beijing has reduced air incursions, but coast guard activity around Taiwan’s outlying islands has become routinized. And since June, Beijing has run standing “law enforcement patrols” east of Taiwan, asserting jurisdiction over the waters Taipei would need in a blockade.

In a recent development, outside of Asia, Beijing has sought to take advantage of anger, particularly in the developing world, at the Trump administration’s “Liberation Day” tariffs and the Iran war. Before traveling to Washington, Xi made a point of stopping in several capitals: he toured Bishkek and Cairo, and attended the BRICS summit in Newly introduced Delhi, stressing that China, not the United States, is now the steadier partner.

Beijing has reason to think this approach is working. It rightly judged that Washington would prioritize keeping the détente alive over responding to its provocations. A year after Busan, China holds a tighter grip on critical supply chains, has set newly introduced precedents in Asia, and faces an adversary in Washington that has grown used to holding back. Beijing likely believes it is better off now than it was when the truce began.

Sources indicate that what looks like success now, however, may still prove to be overreach. In addition to rare earths and magnets, several notable questions went unresolved in past U.S.-Chinese summits and are likely to resurface in this week’s summit in Shenzhen, including China’s anticipated purchases of Boeing aircraft and agricultural products, AI safety, and the United States’ suspension of arms sales to Taiwan. But the most important question is what will become of the current trade truce.

Sources indicate that the United States has complied with the terms of the Busan agreement, suspending the Affiliates Rule and lowering tariffs, but Beijing has throttled the supply of rare-earth minerals and magnets to the United States. U.S. officials say China has delivered only about two-thirds of what it promised, and trade data suggest the shortfall is larger still. The administration believes Beijing’s noncompliance is deliberate. Anecdotal evidence from American business leaders in regular touch with the Ministry of Commerce confirms the administration’s assessment that Beijing seeks to keep a tight leash on rare-earth minerals and will occasionally “yank the chain” on individual companies in response to any perceived slight by Washington.

Industry observers note that from the U.S. perspective, the very point of the Busan negotiations was to avoid this situation. Indeed, the U.S. fact sheet at Busan indicated that China agreed to glitch general licenses for a number of rare earths and other critical minerals to American end people and their suppliers worldwide; case-by-case licenses, which could be delayed by Beijing, would not be required. China has not denied making that commitment, and a few weeks after the summit, the Ministry of Commerce began issuing a upcoming category of general licenses to magnet makers. But Beijing’s licenses have been narrow and firm specific, and American industry continues to face enormous challenges in securing certain rare earths, notably yttrium and scandium.

According to recent reports, beijing’s intention may not be to undermine the Busan agreement but, paradoxically, to strengthen it. In keeping with its belief that strength begets American conciliation, China’s strategy appears to be to occasionally impose shortages to remind Washington of the leverage that Beijing continues to enjoy. But the tactic is beginning to backfire. Shortages of yttrium, used for jet engines and gas turbines, have forced some suppliers to suspend production. Chipmakers are running short of scandium. All of this strengthens the arguments of those who believe Beijing never intended to honor Busan and that the United States should begin to walk away from the agreement. If Washington concludes that China will weaponize rare earths no matter what the United States does, the case for American restraint may fall apart, and with it the détente that has bought Beijing the time it prizes.

Tensions are also mounting in other areas. Each side is increasingly frustrated with the other’s unilateral economic measures and restrictions on technology, particularly those that were not addressed in Busan: for Beijing, U.S. import controls, outbound investment regimes, and licensing backlogs; for Washington, Chinese export controls and State Council directives. A Democratic Congress is less likely to countenance Trump’s China policy and more likely to pursue investigations into China’s espionage and influence efforts and potential malfeasance at the Department of Commerce. The explosive controversy around Huang and Nvidia has the potential to inject fresh tensions into the relationship, particularly on matters related to AI and export controls. The Department of Commerce has already issued a new interim final rule to stop Chinese firms from smuggling chips into China or remotely accessing American AI chips in Southeast Asian data centers. Administration officials insist that closing a loophole China itself claims not to use “should not be something that generates countermeasures.” But Beijing may well retaliate before the rule takes effect in February.

These headwinds make breakthroughs in Shenzhen on purchases, artificial intelligence, nuclear weapons, or Iran less likely. With the truce, extended last week by just two months, set to formally expire on January 10, the summit is one of the last opportunities for Trump and Xi to reach even a modest declaration that they are working to extend the terms set out in Busan and will aim to conclude negotiations in December, when Xi comes to Miami for the G-20 summit.

If China were to continue to throttle rare-earth minerals and magnets, and a January breakdown did come to pass, the two sides might find themselves in another round of escalation. Xi may arrive at the two upcoming summits holding a stronger hand than he did in Busan. But his actions are gradually producing a counterpart with less room—and perhaps less reason—to keep folding.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, over the last few years, some of the most vitriolic debates over Gaza have been about language: the meaning of “intifada,” the implications of “from the river to the sea,” and the importance of using the term “genocide.” Many people criticized protestors for what they believed were extreme or dangerous slogans. Many protestors, in turn, were furious about the shocking chasm between the horrifyingly violent reality they were seeing on social media and the understated, deadening, or deceitful language that political officials and mainstream media were using to describe it.

Industry observers note that two new books offer the opportunity to look back at that surreal period with more certainty. The journalist Akbar Shahid Ahmed’s Crossing the Red Line is the first reported account of what actually took place inside President Joe Biden’s administration during Israel’s war in Gaza, revealing the truth behind its often deceptive public statements. Assal Rad’s Don’t Say Palestine offers a similar dissection of how the media buttressed the government rather than challenged it, clinging to outdated journalistic notions and biases when the horror unfolding before the world demanded something far different.

It has been revealed that over the last few years, some of the most vitriolic debates over Gaza have been about language: the meaning of “intifada,” the implications of “from the river to the sea,” and the importance of using the term “genocide.” Many people criticized protestors for what they believed were extreme or dangerous slogans. Many protestors, in turn, were furious about the shocking chasm between the horrifyingly violent reality they were seeing on social media and the understated, deadening, or deceitful language that political officials and mainstream media were using to describe it.

Sources indicate that two latest books offer the opportunity to look back at that surreal period with more certainty. The journalist Akbar Shahid Ahmed’s Crossing the Red Line is the first reported account of what actually took place inside President Joe Biden’s administration during Israel’s war in Gaza, revealing the truth behind its often deceptive public statements. Assal Rad’s Don’t Say Palestine offers a similar dissection of how the media buttressed the government rather than challenged it, clinging to outdated journalistic notions and biases when the horror unfolding before the world demanded something far different.

Rad, a scholar of Middle Eastern history, begins her book before Oct. 7, 2023. In 2021, she saw a New York Times headline so euphemistic as to be mendacious: “Evictions in Jerusalem Become Focus of Israeli-Palestinian Conflict.” Evictions? “As a historian of the region,” Rad writes, “I was not surprised to see the way the media reflected the official account of their country’s foreign policy positions,” but that didn’t make it less infuriating. Rad posted her marked-up version on social media. It now noted, “Forced expulsions in Jerusalem Become Focus of Palestinian Struggle.”.

Don’t Say Palestine: How the Media Manufactured Consent for Genocide, Assal Rad, Vintage, 256 pp., $20, September 2026.

To Rad, the word “evictions” made ethnic cleansing sound like a real estate dispute or a municipal procedure, and left out the fact that East Jerusalem, where the events were taking place, “is recognized under international law as occupied Palestinian territory.” She knew that this controversy, which was over the Jerusalem neighborhood of Sheikh Jarrah, was representative of the central storyline in the last 150 years of Palestine’s history—a native people dispossessed of their land—and that without the historical context, or the appropriate framing and language, the present-day event made little sense.

It has been revealed that the 2021 riots that ensued when a Jewish settler group claimed these historical Palestinian homes as their own eventually developed into an 11-day war in Gaza. In retrospect, members of the Biden administration should have noticed how the U.S. public responded to this war, in which the Israeli army killed over 250 Palestinians. The officials might have seen that young Americans fresh from the Black Lives Matter movement saw parallels to the Palestinians’ plight, and that global anger at Israel’s brand of asymmetrical violence was growing.

Industry observers note that instead, Biden and team forged ahead, blindly supporting Israel after the Hamas attack on Oct. 7, 2023, with stunningly little awareness of how the American people and the whole world would react. Their obliviousness may have stemmed from a variety of factors: isolation in the Washington bubble, the influence of donors, the belief that Israel was a forever-ally, or a deeper racial bias. What Rad suggests in her clinical, clear-eyed book is that the media played a role in their ignorance as well by parroting the euphemistic, contextless, and factually incorrect language of the U.S. and Israeli governments.

In the aftermath of Oct. 7, Rad began to rewrite headlines more regularly, particularly targeting major outlets such as the Newly introduced York Times, the BBC, Reuters, the Guardian, and the Associated Press. She makes a persuasive case for why headlines are important, even more so in the age of social media and the internet. “Headlines matter because people often do not read beyond them,” she writes. Their passive consumption becomes the everyday wallpaper of readers’ realities.

A panel of Upcoming York Times headlines annotated by Assal Rad. Assal Rad screenshots via Zeteo.

Many readers will be familiar with Rad’s concerns. Critics of the New York Times, for example, have long highlighted the newspaper’s usage of passive voice. Headlines like “Strike on Area Where Displaced Gazans Were Camped Kills Up to 25,” or “Lives Ended in Gaza” also studiously avoid naming the perpetrator. After the shocking killing of the 5-year-old child Hind Rajab—who called for help after the Israeli army fired onto her family’s vehicle, initially killing everyone besides her before fatally shooting her and the emergency workers who came to rescue her—major media outlets such as the BBC, CNN, and the New York Times failed to mention Israel or its army in their headlines. As Rad notes throughout the book, similar headlines about atrocities in Ukraine typically name Russia or Putin. Beyond this, Rad points to the use of chillingly anodyne language that is borrowed from the Israeli or U.S. militaries: “targeted strikes” for “indiscriminate bombings,” or “a humanitarian challenge” for what is in reality “a policy of starvation.”.

In the case of Israel’s wars in the Middle East, Rad exposes how the manipulation of the legal and moral term “self-defense” has come to justify more and more violence. The U.S. and Israeli governments have done this before. What’s been different in recent years, however, is that the reality of Israeli actions  has suddenly become ubiquitous and visible. “For the first time,” Rad writes, “millions around the world watched a genocide unfold live on their phones, uncensored, because of the bravery of Palestinian journalists and the reach of social media.” What Israel was doing—blowing up hospitals, collapsing universities, starving already-food-deprived populations, dropping 2,000-pound bombs on cities, men, women, and children—certainly didn’t look like self-defense.

According to recent reports, yet even when a hospital or school was bombed, the U.S. media often hedged along with the Biden government. It claimed that events still need to be investigated, leaving what people saw with their own eyes to hover in factual limbo. Worse, it would repeat officials’ assertions that, say, bombing a hospital and killing hundreds of people might have been legal because the Israeli army was “targeting Hamas,” a widely repeated phrase that came to be imbued with as much exonerating power as “self-defense.”.

In a recent development, some of these decisions are not easy. Newspapers have a responsibility to break news quickly but never make a single factual error. Israel barred Western journalists from entering Gaza, so in the early weeks of the war newspapers might have been even more cautious before issuing blame for bombings. But ultimately, this led to them to give extraordinary weight to the testimonies of the Israeli army in assessing such ambiguities. Beyond individual incidents, Rad argues that Israel’s war on Gaza should have been framed much earlier as a deliberate campaign of annihilation or genocide, not a war between two equal parties. The laws of war might allow for some morally abhorrent actions by all sides, but those actions look different when they are mere aspects of what was (and remains) a wildly disproportionate campaign.

A photo taken during a controlled tour and subsequently edited under the supervision of the Israeli military shows Israeli soldiers patrolling a road in Rafah in the Gaza Strip on Sept. 13, 2024.Sharon Aronowicz/AFP via Getty Images.

Indeed, it is worth asking why the mainstream media believed anything Israel’s radical, far-right, wholly corrupt government or military said, whether about specific bombings or larger challenges, like the claim it was solely trying to “defeat Hamas.” The tendency to simply relay the arguments of public officials is one of the biggest pitfalls of supposedly objective journalism, especially when it comes to governments that have proven to be autocratic or repressive. I was surprised last year, for example, to see a Upcoming York Times headline that said, “Erdogan Calls It an Anticorruption Drive. His Rivals Call It a Political Crackdown.” Erdogan has been a repressive authoritarian leader since 2013; what is the point of putting his propaganda in the headline?

In Don’t Say Palestine, Rad repeatedly highlights these either/or question headlines. One reason for their popularity may be a boring one: They drive reader engagement. In the case of Gaza, however, it’s possible that the media’s noncommittal headlines betray a deeper, more desperate wish.

As Rad and Ahmed show, Biden’s foreign policy team also seemed desperate to believe in a fantasy version of Israel. Despite the country’s long history of violence against Palestinians, and despite the repeated genocidal statements from high-level Israeli officials, Biden and his team continued to give Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and the Israeli army the benefit of the doubt. For Biden and those around him, Israel remained inherently good, a delusion that might have come naturally to Americans because they believe it about themselves.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu hugs U.S. President Joe Biden upon his arrival at Tel Aviv’s Ben Gurion Airport in Israel on Oct. 18, 2023.Brendan Smiallowski/AFP via Getty Images.

Sources indicate that ahmed, one of the few reporters to consistently break news and pursue stories about Biden’s foreign policy advisors, offers a painstaking, chronological account of the administration’s gross failures in Crossing the Red Line. One of the most key throughlines of Ahmed’s book is how the Biden foreign policy team subverted the very traditional processes of U.S. government, all to maintain their secretive stranglehold on this conflict.

Industry observers note that crossing the Red Line: Biden, His Advisors, and Israel’s War in Gaza, Akbar Shahid Ahmed, W.W. Norton & Co., 368 pp., $31.99, September 2026.

Recent findings suggest that according to Ahmed, Biden’s team demonstrated a “disdain” for their fellow Democrats and government colleagues, sometimes acting like intelligence officers running a covert war in Latin America while swatting away annoying moral and legal restrictions. “Twice in December [2023], Blinken invoked emergency powers to ignore the standard procedures for U.S. arms deals—which involved consultation with Congress,” Ahmed writes, “so that Washington could rush equipment to the Israelis.” Uzra Zeya, who oversaw human rights work at the State Department, discouraged “split memos” in which some officials could oppose a policy that others had endorsed because those memos would put Blinken on record for whatever he decided. The resulting “consensus memos” instead created what another official called “herd immunity,” in which no one could be blamed for the policy.

Recent findings suggest that members of the Biden foreign policy team had been to law school and they knew how to twist legal logic. “For [Jake] Sullivan to claim that lack of proven intent to violate international law precluded Israel’s having committed war crimes,” Ahmed writes, “suggested that the administration could never acknowledge that that occurred.” Those violations were most visible and obvious when it came to military strikes on sites protected by international law, like medical facilities, schools, and houses of worship—all places that Israel would bomb and destroy over time. During the first bombing of Gaza’s Al-Ahli Hospital, “Biden not only declared Israel’s innocence immediately,” Rad notes, “he defined a norm in which Israel could not be guilty because its moral superiority made it incapable of such breaches … The Al-Ahli hospital episode became the model for how the Biden administration would approach the Gaza Genocide. Israel would be taken at its word, exonerated from guilt, and allowed to act with total impunity, with the backing and corroboration of the United States to provide credibility for its actions at every turn.”.

According to recent reports, impunity for abetting war crimes weakens U.S. democracy.

A new book details how the country slayed Washington’s foes.

Recent findings suggest that the conduct of Israel’s bombing campaign was a key element in the International Criminal Court’s case against Prime Minister Netanyahu and former Defense Minister Yoav Gallant. Another was starvation. Using starvation as a method of warfare is a war crime; Human Rights Watch declared that Israel was doing this as early as December 2023. Yet Biden officials publicly doubted humanitarian and intelligence officials, rejecting assessments that would have been taken “as gospel” in other times. When representatives from aid groups met with White House Middle East coordinator Brett McGurk, Ahmed writes, “he surprised them by denying that conditions could worsen.” In a much-talked-about passage, Ahmed writes that both McGurk and Sullivan told others they didn’t think Palestinians were actually starving or looked skinny—something both men deny.

Sources indicate that but the reason this allegation isn’t hard to believe in the context of Ahmed’s book is because an ongoing war with bombing campaigns of stunningly high frequency requires humans to constantly make all kinds of macabre logistical choices and decisions. As long time Middle East hand Aaron David Miller told the Latest Yorker in 2024, Biden did not have the “same depth of feeling and empathy for the Palestinians of Gaza” as he did for Israel. Indeed, the Jerusalem Post revealed this month that during Biden’s last phone call with Netanyahu before leaving the White House, Biden said, “You’re a good man … I admire you. It took a lot of courage to do what you did.”.

Hidaya, a 31-year-old Palestinian mother, carries her sick and malnourished 18-month-old son Mohammed al-Mutawaq inside their tent at the Al-Shati refugee camp, west of Gaza City, on July 24, 2025.Omar Al-Qattaa/AFP via Getty Images.

In a recent development, the idea that Israel was actively trying to starve Gaza was softened by much of the media too, despite Israeli officials’ open declarations of this intent. Rad notes that in the Economist, a story on the threat of famine in Gaza didn’t even mention Israel. In headlines, the Latest York Times asked, “Why Isn’t More Aid Getting to Gazans?” and, “What is a Famine and Who Determines that One Exists?” in March and June 2024, respectively. (Israel has long controlled all food that gets into Gaza as part of its decades-long occupation and blockade.) When Israel’s defense minister Israel Katz stated explicitly that no aid would be allowed into Gaza, major outlets like Reuters posted headlines that uncritically echoed Israel’s official statements like: “Israeli Defense Minister Claims No Humanitarian Aid to Enter Gaza as Tool of Pressure on Hamas.” As Rad contends, this effectively legitimized the use of hunger as a weapon of war. One BBC article said that over the last two years, Palestinians’ access to food had been “complicated.” “The same article repeatedly stated Israeli denials of any wrongdoing, including the government’s rejection of the [Integrated Food Security Phase Classification] report”—the global gold standard of food security assessments. According to the BBC, Israel denied that Israeli soldiers had shot and killed aid seekers, and Netanyahu denied that starvation was taking place at all.

With the normal channels blocked, the Biden administration went to embarrassing lengths to get food to Palestinians, such as building a pier in the sea and airdropping food packages, all to avoid doing the obvious, which was forcing the Israelis to allow food into the strip. The Americans also clung to and broadcast the idea that a ceasefire represented the only way to end Gaza’s suffering. No matter how many times Netanyahu rejected ceasefire terms or petulantly sabotaged them, and even after Israeli press reported Netanyahu’s obvious self-interest in prolonging the war, Biden and his team insisted it was the only way out of the unfolding disaster.

According to recent reports, starting in April 2024, to avoid the ceasefire he never wanted, Netanyahu began targeting people in other countries. First, there was the bombing of the Iranian consulate in Damascus; then, in July, there was the assassination of Ismail Haniyeh inside Iran; and in September, there was the Israeli pager attack on Hezbollah operatives (as well as innocent bystanders) as they went about their daily lives. In rapid succession, the Israelis then killed Hassan Nasrallah and unleashed an astounding bombing campaign on the city of Beirut, as well as a ground invasion into Southern Lebanon. Today, that region has been razed to the ground. Whole villages have been destroyed, 4,300 people have been killed, and more than 1.2 million displaced.

In a recent development, at every horrific turn in Crossing the Red Line, Ahmed stops to remind us that the same day, week, or month that another horror or humiliation occurred, the Biden administration would decide to send more weapons to Israel anyway. “Regardless of the gut-wrenching cost and their mutual disdain,” Ahmed writes, “Netanyahu and Biden might still take credit for a latest Middle East in which Israel held more sway.”.

Palestinians bury relatives killed in overnight Israeli strikes on the Fatima Bint Asad school in Jabalia, at a cemetery in the northern Gaza Strip on May 12, 2025. Bashar Taleb/AFP via Getty Images.

According to recent reports, ahmed argues that careerism and groupthink fueled a lot of the behavior of the Biden team. But his reporting also suggests that strengthening Israel—ensuring that it wins everything—was a goal in itself. For decades, U.S. policy was for Israel to be the strongest country in the Middle East, and in 2025, a U.S. government at last achieved that goal. Israel became the region’s undeniable military heavyweight.

In a recent development, thanks to works like Rad’s and Ahmed’s, the human toll of this policy has become clear to most Americans. Increasingly, newspaper headlines have reflected this reality, too. Here’s a recent one from the Fresh York Times: “Israel Has Committed Genocidal Acts in Gaza Since Cease-Fire, U.N. Human Rights Panel States.” For her part, Rad does not deny that many journalists who have written and reported on the war have done excellent work. The value of her critique is more about these Western publications as a whole – how they often fail to fulfill their most vital professional purpose:  holding the powerful to account.

In a recent development, for the Biden team, the failure of accountability has continued even after leaving office. Confronted with evidence of their culpability in this nightmare, former officials now use opaque and passive language, as if the people who ran the most powerful country in the world simply had no control of events, no control over Netanyahu and no control over President Biden, that sad prisoner of a 1970s sepia-toned fever dream about Golda Meir. As a result, they end up implying that they were merely shirking their moral responsibility to please their aging leader, as if they were functionaries in an authoritarian regime.

It’s possible—in the sense that anything is possible—that these officials were ignorant of what kind of country Israel had become in the last 20 years. Ignorance of cultures and history, after all, was a major engine of the Americans’ failed wars in Iraq and Afghanistan. Moments in Ahmed’s book manage to surprise even him, such as when veteran Middle East diplomat Barbara Leaf cries, “Come on, the IDF doesn’t participate in settler violence!” Perhaps Biden’s team were also victims of decades of misleading or understated media headlines and that was why they continued to give Israeli leaders the benefit of the doubt—or take them at their word. But there is another term for consistently giving the benefit of the doubt to people who share your skin color over people who don’t. In Crossing the Red Line, Ahmed argues that the war on terror conditioned most “U.S. foreign policy professionals” to be comfortable “with jaw-dropping atrocities and dehumanizing of people in the region.” Rad goes back further, to the entire history of Palestine. “The horrors that have been normalized in Gaza,” she writes, “are the culmination of this long history of racism and injustice.”.

Sources indicate that today, Republicans, some Democrats, and probably much of the U.S. security state is still responsible for supporting Netanyahu’s government as it works to destroy Gaza. It was Americans’ own corrupted consensus and Israeli’s murderous one that came together to wreck the international legal order, all while Western media organs chronicled the downfall of that order in careful, hedging tones. One of the most accurate headlines about Gaza, Rad writes, came from the satirical newspaper the Onion following the October 2025 ceasefire announcement: “Israel Agrees to Go Back to Killing Palestinians on Less Frequent Basis.” The advantage of fact-based, active-voiced headlines is that they don’t only tell what’s happening in the present. They tell what will still be happening in the future.

Draft plan to overhaul Smithsonian spotted on White House staffer's laptop: report

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sen. Josh Hawley, R-Mo., discusses controversies surrounding the Smithsonian Institution and President Donald Trump calling on the museum to replace a sculpture with a statue of George Washington on ‘The Ingraham Angle.’.

Photos taken by a commuter on Washington, D.C.'s Metro system appear to show a White House advisor’s laptop displaying a draft strategy to overhaul the Smithsonian’s National Museum of American History, ProPublica reported.

Last month, a commuter riding the Orange Line from Northern Virginia noticed a man in a suit working on a laptop displaying a document titled "Smithsonian Institution Renewal Plan." The commuter photographed the screen and sent the images to ProPublica.

In a recent development, the multipoint draft proposed firing museum Director Anthea Hartig, creating new museum-wide exhibit guidelines that omit the Smithsonian’s diversity style guide, reviewing its traveling-exhibition strategy — including ending "The Bias Inside Us" — and reassessing grants to what the draft called "woke third parties," including the American Alliance of Museums. A separate handwritten note that was also pictured proposed a policy against "X-rated" exhibitions. ProPublica said it likely referred to an exhibit the White House criticized for displaying a two-piece chrome-and-rubber harness designed for sadomasochism.

INSIDE THE BEHEMOTH SMITHSONIAN MUSEUM NETWORK DRAWING FIRE FROM THE TRUMP ADMINISTRATION.

The Smithsonian's National Museum of American History in Washington, D.C., on Oct. 12, 2025. Photos taken on a D.C. Metro train appear to show a White House advisor's laptop displaying a draft initiative to overhaul the museum's leadership, exhibits and K-12 curriculum. (Stefani Reynolds/Bloomberg via Getty Images).

The draft renewal plan pictured on the staffer's laptop surfaced amid a broader Trump administration effort to reshape how the Smithsonian presents American history. The White House released a 162-page report on July 4 accusing the National Museum of American History of "ideological capture." Two congressional hearings followed, and a July executive order directed officials to post signs outside the museum informing visitors of the report’s findings about "ideological capture," though ProPublica reported the signs had not yet gone up as of publication.

Fox News Digital reached out to the White House for comment on the photographed document and whether any of its proposals are under consideration, but did not receive a response by publication. The photographed document does not establish whether the proposals were approved or put into effect.

TRUMP GIVES SMITHSONIAN DAYS TO REPLACE 'STRANGE MODERNIST SCULPTURE' WITH FOUNDING FATHER.

In a recent development, proPublica reported that it identified the White House staffer as Sam Bock, a 27-year-old associate policy advisor with the White House Domestic Policy Council — which produced the July report — after spotting the initials "B.S." or "S.B." on the laptop screen and following a man matching his description from the Metro to a White House employee checkpoint. ProPublica reported that Bock did not respond to its messages and that the Smithsonian declined to comment.

ProPublica reported that the proposals on Bock’s laptop envisioned a permanent exhibit celebrating Western civilization, a display on prominent American families, a large George Washington statue at the museum entrance and new museum-wide interpretive guidelines written without reference to the Smithsonian’s diversity style guide. A separate handwritten note photographed alongside the laptop also floated a potential new D-Day exhibit.

The Smithsonian's National Museum of American History in Washington, D.C.. A July White House report accused the museum of "ideological capture," and a draft renewal plan photographed on a White House advisor's laptop proposed replacing its diversity guidelines and adding a George Washington statue at the entrance. (Kevin Carter).

In addition to the proposed exhibit changes, the draft called for the firing of National Museum of American History Director Anthea Hartig and about a dozen senior administrators and curators. That proposal came as Smithsonian Secretary Lonnie Bunch, who leads the broader institution, was preparing to retire at year’s end. ProPublica reported that White House criticism of the Smithsonian helped prompt Bunch’s departure.

Industry observers note that TRUMP V. SMITHSONIAN: A TIMELINE OF HOW THE WHITE HOUSE FIGHT OVER 'WOKE' HISTORY UNFOLDED.

The draft proposal also called for overhauling the museum’s online curriculum for K-12 students, including dropping a module on immigration and creating latest material focused on the Founders, according to ProPublica, which noted the document floated possible titles for the new curriculum, including "Architects of Liberty" and "Profiles in Liberty.".

It has been revealed that smithsonian Secretary Lonnie Bunch poses for a portrait at the Smithsonian Castle on the National Mall in Washington, D.C., on May 28, 2026. Bunch is preparing to retire at the end of the year amid White House criticism of the institution, according to ProPublica. (Al Drago/The Washington Post via Getty Images).

In a recent development, the administration’s push to reshape how the Smithsonian presents American history began picking up steam in March 2025, when Trump signed an executive order directing Vice President JD Vance, through his role on the Smithsonian’s Board of Regents, to help remove what the order called "improper ideology" from the institution. The Smithsonian, which encompasses 21 museums and D.C.'s National Zoo, is governed by a 17-member Board of Regents that consists of the vice president, the chief justice of the Supreme Court, members of Congress and private citizens. It receives more than $1 billion in federal funding annually.

The White House’s July report cited, among other examples, a museum exhibit that raised the possibility Benjamin Franklin had used enslaved people in his household as subjects in electrical experiments. It also criticized staff training based on a social-action toolkit that the report noted linked museums to White supremacy and other forms of oppression.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP.

The report noted the museum should not erase slavery, Jim Crow or other national failures. Its broader charge was that the museum was not giving visitors a coherent account of how the country developed, including both its achievements and its wrongs.

The criticism from the Trump administration came amid a longer-running debate over how the museum should tell the nation’s story, which has stretched back to at least 2001.

ProPublica reported that in response to earlier criticism, the Smithsonian convened a blue-ribbon commission in 2001, whose 2002 report urged the museum to present a more unified account of American history. The outlet also reported that after George Floyd’s murder in 2020, Bunch and other leaders began an institution-wide reassessment of the Smithsonian’s priorities and how it tells the nation’s story.

#123376. Industry News: America’s Hidden AI Advantage
