⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, MICHAEL C.
  • According to recent reports, in October, U.S.
  • Cynics have grounds for questioning all of Trump’s moves when it comes to Russia and Ukraine.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, MICHAEL C. DESCH is Packey J. Dee Professor of International Relations at the University of Notre Dame and founding Brian and Jeannelle Brady Family Director of the O’Brien Notre Dame International Security Center.

What America Should Give to Make Peace in Ukraine.

According to recent reports, in October, U.S. President Donald Trump sold his eleventh-hour deal to secure diesel from Russian President Vladimir Putin—pausing sanctions that his own administration had imposed—as a boon for the negotiations to end the war in Ukraine. The arrangement, he wrote on Truth Social, was intended to keep Russia at “the bargaining table.” Of course, it was always obvious to observers that the gambit had as much or more to do with bolstering the U.S. economy and stemming a massive victory for the Democrats in this month’s midterm elections, and in that, it failed.

Cynics have grounds for questioning all of Trump’s moves when it comes to Russia and Ukraine. He clearly dislikes Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky and shows a marked preference for illiberal leaders, especially those willing to give him easy wins. Still, a stopped clock can be right twice a day. And concessions such as the fuel deal are exactly what might move Russia and Ukraine closer to peace, even if they are not wholly motivated by public-spiritedness.

Sources indicate that ukraine and its backers in Europe and the United States have long maintained that Russia only responds to sticks. The problem with their argument is that since 2014, and especially since 2022, Moscow has been subjected to nothing but sticks. According to Kaja Kallas, the European Union’s foreign policy chief, the more than 25,000 sanctions imposed on Russia after its full-scale invasion of Ukraine had cost its economy almost $1.5 trillion as of June. And although Trump has backed Ukraine less consistently than U.S. President Joe Biden did, especially in his rhetoric, his administration has still provided significant financial, military, and intelligence support; his CIA has been more aggressive than Biden’s in assisting Ukraine’s offensive and defensive air operations. All of these coercive measures have proved insufficient to compel a change in Putin’s policy or turn the tide in Ukraine’s favor on the battlefield.

European leaders may fret that Trump, now a lame duck and focused on his legacy, will push for a deal on Ukraine that suits the Kremlin’s interests more than their own. But ultimately, this remains a war in which Russia has the advantage. Europe should recognize that its pressure tactics have not worked and welcome the U.S. president’s willingness to throw in a few carrots among the many sticks used to try to beat the Kremlin into submission. Washington, meanwhile, should continue to pursue a concessionary strategy by encouraging Ukraine to surrender territory, freezing NATO’s expansion, and offering sanctions relief to Moscow. Putin has shown a willingness to sign favorable deals in the past, including the Minsk agreements in 2014 and 2015, which promised an end to the civil conflict in Donbas only to collapse under the duress of Kyiv and European capitals. A more enduring peace is desperately needed in Ukraine, however unfair the price may seem.

According to recent reports, ukraine has had some recent success on the battlefield. Early in 2026, Kyiv launched offensives in western Zaporizhzhia that erased a year of Russian gains there. During the summer, the Ukrainian military embarked on a major counteroffensive, Operation Vivaldi, that made significant progress near Liman, delaying Russia’s campaign to take the Donbas fortress cities of Kramatorsk and Sloviansk. And after four years, Ukrainian forces have finally inflicted serious, albeit not irreparable, damage to the bridge connecting Crimea and Russia, disrupting a military transport route and tarnishing a potent symbol of Putin-era expansionism. Kyiv has also brought the war home to segments of the Russian public with its attacks on oil infrastructure and commercial targets such as warehouses for Wildberries, Russia’s largest online retailer. Supporters in Western capitals have trumpeted these achievements as evidence that Ukraine has turned the tide in a war that previously seemed to be moving in Moscow’s favor.

But tactical wins do not necessarily add up to strategic victory. And as Undersecretary of Defense for Policy Elbridge Colby reminded the Ukraine Defense Contact Group at a meeting earlier this month, the war will be decided on the ground. Casualties remain a huge problem for Ukraine. The few times Zelensky has addressed them, he has offered implausibly low figures for his side and cited astronomically high losses on the other. A recent study by Alexander Grable, a King’s College London war studies researcher, dissects these figures and concludes that Ukraine is suffering far higher casualties than Russia in absolute numbers—findings that, if true, refute the canard that Russia is uniquely careless with the lives of its soldiers. These days, while Ukraine pursues costly offensives to temporarily recover territory, Russia is taking cities and densely fortified areas by encirclement rather than frontal assault, reducing the risk to its fighters.

According to recent reports, although Ukraine’s strikes on Russian oil infrastructure have disrupted refining and strained domestic fuel supplies, Moscow has managed to cushion the blow through emergency measures and rapid repairs. In May, the U.S. Defense Intelligence Agency concluded that Kyiv’s long-range drone attacks did not “substantially affect Russian energy production,” which may explain why the Russian civilian population has not felt the full bite of them. The average Russian seems to be weathering this pain with something between resigned stoicism and increased determination to see the war through to victory. If Ukraine’s deep strikes were designed to encourage the United States to support Zelensky’s proposal for an energy truce, its effects have been counterproductive: higher oil prices have refilled the Kremlin’s war chest and greater energy costs are undermining allied support for Ukraine, especially in the United States.

According to recent reports, many Western battlefield analyses suggest that Russia has recently lost a bit of ground. In fact, the battle lines in Ukraine remain ambiguous. According to the widely followed Military Summary Telegram channel, which applies a nuanced metric of territorial control to geolocated videos from Russian and Ukrainian sources, Russia has continued to make inroads through October and November. In the north, its troops have carved out a buffer zone on the border, making gains around Sumy and Velykyi Burluk. The see-saw battle for Kupyiansk—a fiercely contested gateway to Kharkiv and northeastern Ukraine—once again favors Moscow. In Donetsk, Russian forces have largely taken the city of Dobropillia, which could enable them to creep north behind the Donbas fortress cities and encircle them. And Russia continues to gain ground in eastern Zaporizhzhia, where its units are now edging closer to the region’s administrative capital. Operation Vivaldi may have slowed the Russian advance north of Kramatorsk, but only at a significant cost to some of Ukraine’s best units. Much like the Kursk campaign in 2024, the counteroffensive seems more like a temporary media victory than a real change in the ground war.

In the air, Russia has commenced a deep strike campaign across Ukraine, using drones and ballistic missiles to turn the tables in key regions. Russian forces have severely disrupted Kyiv’s Black Sea operations, intensified strikes against data centers and electricity infrastructure, attacked locomotives, and hit targets ever closer to Ukraine’s western borders, and are now going after major bridges across the Dnieper, which could literally cut the country in two. Russia’s quantitative and qualitative advantage in jet-powered drones allows these weapons to function as effectively as cruise missiles, and recent air operations have been more sustained and systematic as a result. Ukraine’s dearth of American-made PAC-3 interceptor missiles—a result of the United States’ own dwindling defense stockpiles—means that Russian ballistic missiles are mostly unstoppable.

According to recent reports, in October, Trump angrily wrote on social media that Zelensky “doesn’t want to end this war, and probably never did.” This was unfair: undoubtedly, Zelensky does want to end it, just on his own terms. The aid and support Europe and the United States have lavished on Ukraine—initially necessary for preventing a catastrophic defeat—now gives its president little incentive to make peace any other way. Early in the current war, when Ukraine was unexpectedly prevailing on the battlefield, it passed on two promising peace tracks that might have ended the fighting soon after it began.

It has been revealed that but negotiations are now the only way forward for Ukraine, and they will not progress by targeting Russia exclusively with sticks. To overcome the current impasse, Ukraine and its supporters have to put their chips on the table. That means forgoing any hope of NATO accession—or of a sustained NATO military presence in Ukraine—and relinquishing territory to Russia. If Kyiv remains unwilling to make the concessions demanded of losing parties in war, then Washington can take steps to encourage better judgement. The United States could taper down or cut off certain services and munitions it provides the Ukrainian armed forces, including Starlink and Starshield satellite connectivity, Patriot missile defense systems, and intelligence support for air defense and deep strikes on Russian targets. Any of these deprivations would be felt immediately on the battlefield.

In a recent development, washington should offer carrots of its own accord, too. Trump can lift some sanctions, such as those banning Russian commercial flights from U.S. airspace, without much controversy. Lifting others, such as those restricting fossil fuel exports and financial transactions, will be less palatable but more attractive to Russia and thus more effective. Russia’s readmission to the SWIFT interbank messaging service and other global commercial networks must be pursued accordingly.

Pro-Ukrainian hard-liners argue that no amount of carrots will be enough to satisfy Putin’s voracious appetite for territory. They warn that if Russia is not stopped in Ukraine, it will continue its campaign of conquest farther west through Poland, Lithuania, Latvia, Estonia, and beyond, with no end in sight. As Zelensky warned European leaders at the Berlin Security Conference in early November, the Russian military buildup is not just directed at his country, “it is directed against you.” But although Russia is making grinding progress on the fronts in eastern Ukraine, at the rate of its advances in 2025 and this year, it would take three decades just to capture the rest of Ukraine east of the Dnieper. And the idea that Russia, with a military of under 1.6 million men and women in uniform, could defeat a NATO alliance boasting 3.65 million soldiers is implausible, especially considering NATO’s overwhelming advantages in major weapons and military spending.

Even if Russia could take on NATO directly, it is far from clear that Putin wants to. The Kremlin’s war aims in Ukraine may not seem just, but they are narrower than many analysts allege. Since his 2007 speech in Munich excoriating the United States’ global hegemony—and after the 2008 NATO summit declaration that welcomed eventual membership for Georgia and Ukraine—NATO expansion has been Putin’s idée fixe. He has been similarly preoccupied with the status of the pro-Russia citizens of Eastern Ukraine and devoted substantial effort to ensuring protection of their linguistic rights and political influence through the Minsk agreements. Only when that failed did Moscow recognize the two regions of the Donbas, Luhansk and Donetsk as independent states eligible for membership in the Russian Federation, paving the way for direct Russian intervention in the region. Nonetheless, Putin continued to pursue a negotiated solution to the conflict through Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan and Israel’s then Prime Minister Naftali Bennett. As with the Minsk process, it was Ukraine and its backers who walked away from these negotiations when their aims—the complete liberation of all Russian-occupied territory—still appeared achievable on the battlefield.

In a round of U.S.-led peace talks earlier this month in Abu Dhabi, Russia made maximalist demands, asking for the pullback of NATO forces from Poland and the Baltic states, limits on European nuclear deterrence, and restrictions on the size and capabilities of Ukraine’s military. But read in the broader context of Putin’s singular and consistent fixations, these demands look more like negotiating ploys than dealbreakers. It has long been clear what the Kremlin will settle for: control over Ukraine’s eastern border regions and a largely demilitarized Kyiv. Whatever the ultimate terms of this deal, some basic facts are clear. There is no going back to a Ukrainian Donbas, or a Ukrainian Crimea or Novorossiya. And whatever security guarantees Europe and the United States give Ukraine in the future, they cannot include NATO membership.

Sources indicate that the status quo in Ukraine is unsustainable. Four years of war have lulled many of Kyiv’s supporters into complacency about the risk that continued pressure on Russia could create an escalatory spiral. There is increasingly cavalier talk in some newer NATO capitals, for example, about undertaking aggressive NATO exercises near Kaliningrad and overcoming the city’s air and missile defenses. But those steps may only further widen and deepen the war. The clear and present danger of vertical and horizontal escalation must not be dismissed.

It has been revealed that cracks are already showing in the West’s united front against Russia. France and other western European states are experiencing heightened social and political unrest, fueled in part by the costs of the war. In late October, Finnish President Alexander Stubb and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store made a rare phone call to Putin to “convey messages directly regarding future negotiations” toward peace, according to a statement released by the two leaders. In the United States, a once bipartisan hard line toward Russia is starting to fall out of favor, even among Democrats. In mid-October, Democratic Representative Jim Himes told the Warsaw Security Forum that a future Democratic president will have to acknowledge the “tectonic fact” that the United States can no longer afford to play its historic leading role in confronting Russia.

Recent findings suggest that there is reason to think that the Trump administration’s more conciliatory approach has already opened the door to diplomacy. The Oleshky truce brokered by First Lady Melania Trump and the Vatican successfully evacuated civilians trapped in a Russian-occupied city south of Kherson. And the president’s comments in his 60 Minutes interview this month suggested that he is ready to ply Russia with the incentives necessary to get a deal over the line. These are steps in the right direction, but in addition to altering the balance of carrots offered to Russia, the Trump administration must consider providing Ukraine security guarantees outside of the NATO framework.

Sources indicate that now in the twilight of his political career, Trump has made clear his desire to leave a legacy in the form of Nobel Peace Prizes and triumphal arches. Ending a major war in Ukraine would be a crowning achievement, which is why he has waxed lyrical about a “big, beautiful agreement” since he entered his second term in office. And if Trump still believes that China is the pacing threat of the twenty-first century, reintegrating Russia into the global economy and weakening the axis between Putin and Chinese leader Xi Jinping will be paramount for advancing his long-term political vision.

Sources indicate that no one has lost money betting against peace in Ukraine since 2014, and it would be foolhardy to expect Trump to pursue diplomacy solely for altruistic reasons. But perhaps if he sees peace as being in his own interest, as well as that of the United States, he might, despite himself, broker an end to a bloody and increasingly fruitless war. Doing so could be one of the few positive legacies of his second term, even if it does not get him to Oslo.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Welcome to Foreign Policy’s China Brief.

The highlights this week: Jensen Huang’s return to Nvidia highlights the reality of U.S.-China relations, the Chinese Communist Party purges another Politburo member, and a beloved China correspondent is remembered.

Welcome to Foreign Policy’s China Brief.

The highlights this week: Jensen Huang’s return to Nvidia highlights the reality of U.S.-China relations, the Chinese Communist Party purges another Politburo member, and a beloved China correspondent is remembered.

U.S. President Donald Trump’s lobbying for Jensen Huang’s return as Nvidia CEO is a national security scandal of unprecedented proportions, as I wrote on Monday (gift link).

Huang’s reinstatement comes less than a week after the trilateral summit among Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping, and Russian President Vladimir Putin, in which Trump pronounced the Chinese autocrat his personal friend and endorsed his geopolitical language.

Taken together, these events illustrate an increasingly clear reality of U.S.-China relations: Beijing knows Trump’s pressure points and isn’t afraid to exploit them. But Washington cannot do the same to Xi.

It is difficult to know how much Xi shaped Trump’s thinking on Huang. Trump was already sympathetic to Huang and receptive to the whispers of Silicon Valley leaders. But the U.S. president himself mentioned he had discussed the matter with Xi; whatever the precise chain of influence, China scored a major win.

It has been revealed that trump’s obsequiousness toward Xi reflects China’s skillful use of both stick and carrot. Last year, Beijing’s rare-earth squeeze caused panic in Washington and forced Trump into a humiliating climbdown in the tariff war that he started. Trump’s involvement in reinstating Huang was likely triggered in part by another of the president’s fears: a falling stock market.

Industry observers note that with the U.S. economy still entangled with China, Xi has the leverage to force supply-chain crises across multiple industries. He can also offer Trump praise and pageantry on the world stage to help compensate for unpopularity on the home front.

Washington, by contrast, lacks the will, knowledge, and capability to pressure Beijing. The Trump administration is bogged down in Iran, has gutted U.S. cybersecurity capabilities, and has wrecked the relationships that once gave allies the confidence to push back against China. With the Nvidia scandal, it has shown that it will abandon its own sanctions enforcement under pressure.

It’s this imbalance of power that makes me skeptical of recent announcements that there will be another round of U.S. tariffs on China. As much as Trump loves tariffs, he wants Xi’s approval more.

Some analysts, eager to avert a so-called second Cold War, have embraced Trump’s support for reinstating Huang, on the grounds that U.S. chip policy toward China should be more permissive. This misses the point entirely. As I have argued, the real debate about U.S. chip policy needed to be held in good faith.

Trump’s decision to allow high-end chip exports to China was not the result of careful deliberation, but of straightforward corruption.

Those celebrating Huang’s return are overlooking more than the blatant violations of national-security norms, the abandonment of serious sanctions enforcement, and Trump’s personal financial interest in Nvidia. They are also ignoring the lessons of the recent past.

It has been revealed that china hawks made a moral and strategic blunder by backing Trump during his first term when his interests seemed aligned with theirs. It would be even more foolish for China doves to do the same today.

According to recent reports, politburo member purged. On Tuesday, Xi purged yet another senior official: Shanghai party chief Chen Jining. As is customary, the news broke with an announcement that Chen was under investigation for severe violations of Chinese Communist Party (CCP) discipline. His fall brings the number of Politburo members eliminated since last year to four, out of an original 24 members in 2022.

Unlike most of his contemporaries, Chen is a genuine intellectual. An environmental engineer with a Ph.D. from Imperial College London, he followed an unusual path to the top, serving as president of the prestigious Tsinghua University before becoming minister of environmental protection in 2015. As mayor of Beijing from 2017 to 2022, he played an vital role in cleaning up the city’s notoriously polluted air.

Sources indicate that publicly, Chen has been loyal to Xi, so why was he purged? My guess is that Xi has become increasingly paranoid about the emergence of potential successors. Perhaps he heard one too many people praise Chen’s intelligence and management skills.

Whatever the explanation, the purge points to a crisis in the CCP’s leadership. The question is whether that reflects genuine opposition to Xi or exists entirely in the leader’s imagination.

In a recent development, GOP’s Huang fallout. Republican Party pushback against Huang’s reinstatement at Nvidia has been surprisingly strong. Senators and influential figures such as Mitt Romney have come out against the decision and called for further investigation. Unless Trump intimidates them into submission, Nvidia could face scrutiny that may intensify once the new U.S. Congress takes office in January.

Huang is scheduled to testify publicly before Congress on Dec. 3, and even if Nvidia has seemingly secured a reprieve from federal investigation for now, it may have set itself up as an easy target for whatever presidential administration takes office in 2029.

Recent findings suggest that ‘Guaranteed bubble’ phenomenon. One aspect of the Nvidia scandal that has received little attention is how closely it resembles the way China treats private companies: protecting favorites and punishing those that fall out of favor. Trump has far less ability to intervene as freely as the CCP, but the parallels are worth noting.

In China, this kind of state interference helped create a phenomenon called the “guaranteed bubble.” The government has repeatedly stepped in to prop up companies when their troubles threaten to cause public unrest or economic insecurity. This created an expectation that these firms were too substantial to fail and therefore safe investments.

Industry observers note that that confidence inflated the bubble further until reality caught up. Even if the artificial intelligence boom does not go that way, Trump’s interference threatens a long-standing U.S. advantage over China: trust that stock prices represent genuine value and that corporate failings are not being covered up by the state.

Robert Foyle Hunwick, a long-term China correspondent and a close friend of mine, died last week at 47 after a short battle with cancer. A British journalist who moved to China in the late 2000s, Rob wrote about society, crime, and nightlife in China and its neighbors for numerous outlets, including Foreign Policy.

Sources indicate that he loved both the humanity and the chaos of modern Chinese life and reserved some of his sharpest criticism for Western journalists who thought themselves above it all. He will be deeply missed.

James Palmer is a deputy editor at Foreign Policy. Bluesky: @beijingpalmer.bsky.social.

Kilmar Abrego Garcia lands in Madrid, Spain, after leaving the United States voluntarily amid a deportation fight.

Kilmar Ábrego García, the illegal immigrant from El Salvador whose case became a flashpoint for critics of President Donald Trump's immigration enforcement policies, landed in Spain on Wednesday after agreeing to leave the United States.

Ábrego García departed Tuesday for Madrid on a commercial flight and was swarmed with supporters and journalists after touching down and making his way through the airport.

His voluntary departure ends his battle with the Trump administration that began last year with his initial deportation over allegations that he was a member of the MS-13 gang. He ultimately aims to make his way to Mexico, The New York Times reported, citing his attorneys.

"Kudos to the president, the Department of Homeland Security and Stephen Miller, who have been adamant about what's doing what's right.".

Industry observers note that A federal judge in Maryland ordered Ábrego García to leave the U.S. by Tuesday, according to two sources familiar with the matter. That order remains under seal, and the exact terms of his release were not immediately clear.

The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) emphasized that Ábrego García did not receive any financial incentives through the Trump administration's voluntary self-deportation program, which offers migrants travel assistance and financial support to leave the country.

"To be clear: Kilmar Abrego Garcia departed the United States pursuant to a removal order. He paid for his own flight and received no incentives," DHS posted on X. "He will NEVER be allowed back inside the United States.".

According to recent reports, the move comes after sustained efforts by the Trump administration to remove Ábrego García, who entered the U.S. illegally more than a decade ago. At one point during the legal proceedings, federal authorities sought to deport him to several African nations, one of them being Liberia.

He was subsequently deported to El Salvador in error and held in the Central American nation's maximum-security CECOT prison despite a standing court order barring his removal there due to the risk of gang persecution.

Democrats rallied around him despite his suspected ties to the MS-13 gang.

The Paradox of Iranian Power

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 23 min read (4671 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foreignaffairs

⏱️ ~23 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Iran’s theocratic rulers have drawn a Nietzschean lesson from nearly half a century of crises: what has not killed their revolution has only made it stronger.
  • They are not entirely misguided in that belief.
  • The joint U.S.-Israeli war on Iran did not meaningfully rally an impoverished and abused Iranian society around its oppressive regime.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Why the Islamic Republic Can’t Make Peace.

Iran’s theocratic rulers have drawn a Nietzschean lesson from nearly half a century of crises: what has not killed their revolution has only made it stronger. In 2026, the Islamic Republic survived a nationwide uprising and a devastating war with the United States and Israel that eliminated its leaders, decimated its military, and ravaged its economy. Yet rather than reconsider the principles and policies that have stoked nearly five decades of confrontation, isolation, and popular unrest, Tehran’s rulers drew the opposite conclusion: revolutionary ideology was not an albatross weighing the regime down, but a life preserver keeping it afloat.

They are not entirely misguided in that belief. Since the 1979 revolution transformed Iran from a pro-American monarchy into an anti-American theocracy, the regime’s organizing principles have been the imposition of theocratic rule at home and resistance against Israel and the United States abroad. These policies have fueled recurring internal unrest and external conflicts that have impoverished, isolated, and destabilized Iran. Paradoxically, however, revolutionary regimes that survive such challenges often emerge more resilient, cohesive, and confident in their ideological convictions. The Islamic Republic, under the newly introduced leadership of Mojtaba Khamenei, appears to be following the same pattern.

The joint U.S.-Israeli war on Iran did not meaningfully rally an impoverished and abused Iranian society around its oppressive regime. It did, however, rally the regime around the revolution. Rather than embrace the possibility of a different political order, Tehran’s rulers closed ranks and extended the Khamenei era—literally, by anointing Mojtaba Khamenei to succeed his father, the slain supreme leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei. “God’s grace is clear,” supporters chanted, “A young Khamenei is here!”.

At home, the war entrenched a revolutionary elite whose priority is resistance, not governance. That will only prolong the country’s crisis. The regime can suppress revolts but cannot address the conditions that produce them, leaving Iran trapped in a downward spiral of despotism, decline, and despair.

U.S. President Donald Trump’s attempt to resolve the Iranian challenge instead exacerbated it. The war, rolled out in the midst of negotiations, has degraded Tehran’s military capabilities but hardened its revolutionary character, deepened its already profound mistrust of Washington, and taught its rulers a dangerous lesson: violence, not dialogue, secures concessions. Tehran has established upcoming precedents for attacking its neighbors, disrupting global energy supplies, and asserting control over the Strait of Hormuz. Its leaders are determined to rebuild their military capabilities and avenge Khamenei’s death, while Israel is equally determined to prevent Iran from restoring the capacity to threaten it. What Tehran may regard as necessary to rebuild its deterrence, Israel may regard as preparation for another war.

Industry observers note that washington can choose to end its war with Iran, but it cannot end the Islamic Republic’s confrontation with the United States. Israel cannot afford to ignore an adversary it regards as an existential threat. Gulf Arab states may have little say in whether Israel and Iran fight another war, but they could bear some of its greatest costs as their cities, energy infrastructure, and shipping through the Strait of Hormuz are vulnerable to Iranian retaliation. Tehran regards the Gulf’s economic and technological achievements not as examples to emulate, but as vulnerabilities to exploit and targets to threaten. For these reasons, the end of this war is likely to prove an intermission rather than a resolution.

Recent findings suggest that the challenges the Islamic Republic poses to the Middle East, the United States, and the global economy can ultimately be resolved only with political change in Tehran. Yet getting through 2026 has simply reinforced the Islamic Republic’s revolutionary conviction that its survival is best ensured through continuity, not change. The country will remain suspended between war and peace abroad, and between prolonged decay and sudden upheaval at home. Iran is thus left in a paradox. Revolutionary ideology has led the country toward destruction. But abandoning revolutionary ideology could lead the regime toward collapse.

According to recent reports, like all ailing autocracies, the Islamic Republic has the potential to both gradually atrophy or abruptly implode. Russian Tsar Nicholas I first referred to the Ottoman Empire as “the sick man” of Europe in 1853; its end came seven decades later. George Kennan wrote in these pages in 1947 that the Soviet Union “bears within it the seeds of its own decay, and that the sprouting of these seeds is well advanced.” It took another 44 years for the Soviet Union to collapse.

In a recent development, the Islamic Republic of Iran has come to resemble the Leaning Tower of Pisa: seemingly on the verge of collapse but defying political gravity decade after decade. Despite its abundant natural resources and human capital, theocratic Iran has been a case study in squandered national potential. Its economy is trapped in recurring crises, its currency is ravaged by inflation, and generations of educated citizens seek their futures abroad. Nearly half a century after the revolution, Iran’s real GDP per capita remains nearly a quarter below its 1976 peak. That means that many Iranians are materially worse off than their parents and grandparents were before the revolution, an economic regression typically suffered only by failed states or societies ravaged by civil war.

While Iran’s economy has regressed, its society has progressed. Over the last five decades, its population has nearly tripled, and a predominantly rural and traditional society has become increasingly urban, educated, and socially liberal. Since the 2022–23 “Woman, Life, Freedom” protests, mandatory veiling—what Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini once called the “flag” of the Islamic Revolution—appears increasingly unenforceable. Women now routinely walk down the streets of Tehran and other cities with their hair uncovered. The breaking of this taboo will embolden Iranians to break others. In short, Iran’s citizens look forward, Iran’s rulers look backward, and Iran’s economy spirals downward. It is a country whose people have moved beyond the revolution, but whose rulers refuse to leave it behind.

The historian Crane Brinton compared revolutions to fevers that eventually break, ushering in a period of moderation known as Thermidor. Yet many decades after the revolution, Iran’s rulers still refuse to lower the temperature. Iranian society has long sought a return to normalcy, but the regime fears that ending the revolution would mean ending its own rule. The growing gap between rulers and the ruled can be sustained only through continued brutality. The Islamic Republic’s aspiring Deng Xiaopings were sidelined for fear they might become the regime’s Mikhail Gorbachevs. Its Vaclav Havels have been imprisoned, exiled, or killed. Edmund Burke warned that “a state without the means of some change is without the means of its conservation.” Yet the Islamic Republic’s rulers appear more willing to risk breaking the regime than to allow themselves to bend, and more willing to risk another calamitous war than to abandon the revolutionary principles that have sustained their power.

Revolutionary regimes are surprisingly resilient. As the political scientists Steven Levitsky and Lucan Way write in Revolution and Dictatorship, such regimes tend to last nearly three times as long as their nonrevolutionary counterparts, despite being twice as likely to be involved in wars. Although their radicalism often triggers counterrevolution or external war, regimes that survive those early challenges commonly develop three pillars of durability: “a cohesive ruling elite,” “a highly developed and loyal coercive apparatus,” and “the destruction of rival organizations and alternative centers of power in society.”.

According to recent reports, the Islamic Republic has developed these three pillars because of, not in spite of, decades of internal opposition and near-constant hot and cold wars. The 444-day seizure of the U.S. embassy in Tehran beginning in 1979 and the eight-year war with Saddam Hussein’s Iraq, which began the following year, were foundational crises that brought international isolation and economic devastation to Iran but helped entrench Khomeini’s theocracy. Both were prolonged well beyond their initial objectives, in part because they served the regime’s internal consolidation: the hostage crisis marginalized moderates, while the exigencies of the war with Iraq smothered internal dissent and helped build the military-industrial system—namely the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC)—to entrench theocratic government. Just as the Long March forged the bonds and credentials of China’s revolutionary elite in the 1930s, the Iran-Iraq War of the 1980s forged those of the Revolutionary Guard commanders who rule Iran today.

Industry observers note that whereas most states seek normalcy and the resolution of crises, crises in the Islamic Republic provided fertile soil for the revolution. As Abolhassan Bani-Sadr, the Islamic Republic’s first president, observed in 2003, after more than two decades in exile: “With the end of the war, crisis-making did not end. The mullahs’ regime, which was born of crisis-making, could not continue its life without making crises.” The Islamic Republic has made disequilibrium its equilibrium. Indeed, some within the regime privately believe that IRGC attacks on shipping during this year’s cease-fire, as well as the maximalist demands of Iranian negotiators, were meant to prolong the war and entrench the power of hard-liners, much as the Iran-Iraq War helped cement their position.

By attacking Iran weeks after the regime killed thousands of protesters, one of the bloodiest massacres in modern Iranian history, Trump provided Tehran with an external crisis to divert attention from its internal one. Imagine if the United States had attacked the Soviet Union in 1982, as its economy stagnated, its ideology languished, and its aging rulers struggled to preserve a discredited political order. Rather than hastening communism’s demise, such an attack might have revitalized its defenders, discredited its critics, and transformed a crisis of legitimacy into a struggle for national survival. Something similar seems to have happened in Iran. The war allowed Tehran’s rulers to portray their decades of hostility toward the United States not as the source of Iran’s predicament, but as vindication of their worldview. It is telling that while Israeli and U.S. forces have killed many of the regime’s top political and military leaders, no high-level officials have defected.

No one in today’s Islamic Republic has the stature to push for reform or rapprochement with Washington; its many veto men, whose privileges depend on the status quo, have the power to block both. Profound change requires consensus. Inertia can be entrenched by a few.

A great deal depends on the largely invisible Mojtaba Khamenei. It remains to be seen for how long the Islamic Republic’s political and military elite will defer to a supreme leader who has, for whatever reason, withdrawn from public view. Iranian political culture tends toward personality cults, and over much of the last century the country has largely been led by four strongmen: Reza Shah (1925 to 1941), Mohammad Reza Shah Pahlavi (1941 to 1979), Khomeini (1979 to 1989), and Ali Khamenei (1989 to 2026). Few major countries have experienced such extraordinary continuity of personal rule across radically different political systems. The present situation—an absent supreme leader hidden from public view, possibly for health reasons or out of fear of assassination, and competing centers of power within the security establishment—therefore looks like an unstable equilibrium.

Sources indicate that after Khomeini came to power, in 1979, outside observers commonly assumed Iran’s revolutionary fervor would fade and that the country’s new leaders could be won over with the right mix of respect and economic inducements. “Khomeini will be somewhat of a saint when we get over the panic,” Andrew Young, a UN ambassador in the Carter administration, predicted in February 1979. “In two years, our relations with Iran will be on a pretty even keel.” But today, the regime still chants “Death to America.” Governments do not cling to policies that they believe endanger their survival. The enduring mistake has been to assume that Iran’s leaders cannot possibly mean what they repeatedly say.

Recent findings suggest that the Islamic Republic has always framed its conflict with the United States not merely as a geopolitical dispute but also as a moral and ideological struggle. Khomeini, who outlined his vision of Islamic government nearly a decade before the revolution and implemented it after seizing power, called the United States “the foremost enemy of Islam” in his last will and testament. His successor, Ali Khamenei, maintained remarkable ideological consistency over nearly four decades, repeatedly describing the rivalry as an “inherent conflict—an inherent incompatibility.” For both men, their publicly articulated convictions proved a far more reliable guide to the Islamic Republic’s conduct than the reassurances of its diplomats or the wishful interpretations of Western observers.

Khamenei’s son and successor Mojtaba—whose face and voice have not been seen or heard since he became supreme leader in March 2026—has echoed his father in his public pronouncements. “The criminal rulers of America and the illegitimate Zionist regime,” he said in one statement, “are not merely enemies of the Islamic Republic, Iran, or the vast front of Islamic resistance; they harbor enmity toward the entire Islamic ummah”—the Muslim community. After the Democratic victories in the U.S. midterm elections in November, a post on Mojtaba Khamenei’s official English-language X account proclaimed that “the process of the US’s collapse has accelerated.” He further warned that neither American elections nor Iranian concessions would alter the “hegemonic system” of the United States and its hostility toward the Islamic Republic.

The elder Khamenei’s assassination at the start of the war continued the transformation of Iran from a country led by clerics into one dominated by current and former IRGC officers. Many observers assumed this shift from turbans to uniforms would move the regime’s focus from religious ideology to national interest. This has yet to happen. Although the regime has adopted more overtly nationalist rhetoric, it still subordinates the welfare and security of Iranians to the goals of the revolution. The motivations of security officials may be more financial than theological, but their interests have remained bound to the same revolutionary order.

According to recent reports, siamak Namazi, an Iranian American who spent nearly eight years as a hostage of the IRGC in Tehran’s Evin prison, describes the Islamic Republic as a “competitive kleptocracy masquerading as a theocracy.” Many of the regime’s elite, he has observed, are driven less by religious dogma than by the spoils of power: preferential exchange rates, privileged loans, import licenses, and a cut of the smuggling trade. “The revolutionary Kool-Aid,” he stated, “is reserved for the ranks, because someone still has to believe enough to open fire on their own countrymen.” The true believers also have a great deal to lose. A January 2026 Bloomberg report alleged that Mojtaba Khamenei had used a middleman to build a financial empire in the West, including $138 million in British luxury real estate and Swiss bank accounts.

It has been revealed that the IRGC has eclipsed the clergy in both political and economic power, with some estimates suggesting they control more than a third of Iran’s economy. Individual commanders have accumulated fortunes, often by enabling the business activities of their children, known as aghazadehs, or princelings. Yet rather than challenge the supreme leader, the senior command’s public statements suggest continued solidarity with the office. Mohsen Rezaei, a longtime IRGC commander with substantial family business interests who returned to serve as secretary of the Supreme National Security Council, expressed his devotion to Mojtaba in a September 2026 interview with state television. “Let us preserve our unity,” he insisted. “Let us preserve our dignity. Let us march behind the leader of the revolution.”.

In a 26-page open letter to the American people published the same month, the IRGC declared that the war had “reinvigorated the Islamic Republic” and would ensure the regime’s survival for decades. Rather than question the ideology that had brought Iran to this precipice, the corps reaffirmed velayat-e faqih, the doctrine of clerical guardianship, as an “embodiment of all godly virtues in the political sphere” that empowered Iran to stand firm against diabolical powers. Revolutionary and religious dogma were not the source of Iran’s predicament, they concluded, but rather the “main factors underpinning Iran’s victory.”.

Industry observers note that iran’s rulers are neither pragmatic nationalists guided by traditional state interests nor an apocalyptic death cult. They outsource the politics of martyrdom to regional militias while ruthlessly practicing the politics of survival at home. For the true believers, abandoning the revolution would mean betraying their convictions; for its profiteers, it would mean jeopardizing their power and privileges. When the regime’s survival is at stake, they may change their tactics, but they won’t change their worldview.

Sources indicate that the war has left Tehran both weaker and much more aggressive. Before the war, the Islamic Republic resembled a zombie regime: its ideology, legitimacy, and its 86-year-old supreme leader all appeared to be fading. Since the outbreak of the war, it has come to resemble a gangster regime—one that practices extortion as statecraft—and is emboldened to attack its neighbors, the global economy, and the United States to extract concessions.

Tehran has been rewarded for its defiance by Trump. In his dramatic address launching the war in February 2026, Trump vowed to end Iran’s nuclear weapons ambitions, destroy its missile capabilities, and neutralize its regional proxies. He encouraged Iranians to overthrow their “wicked” dictatorship. But the president soon changed his tune. Although Trump believed the war would be a swift “little excursion,” Iran’s attacks on tankers in the Strait of Hormuz and its over 6,700 missile and drone attacks on its Gulf neighbors compelled him to attempt one of the most striking reversals in modern American foreign policy.

According to recent reports, in June, Trump signed a memorandum of understanding with Tehran that gave away the store. He pledged to lift all sanctions as part of a final agreement, release frozen Iranian assets, permit Iranian oil exports, and work with regional partners on a $300 billion reconstruction package. The agreement also accepted an Iranian role in determining the future administration of the Strait of Hormuz, committed Washington to noninterference in Iran’s internal affairs, and made no mention of Iran’s missiles or regional proxies.

In just four months, Trump had gone from pursuing the most hawkish Iran policy ever to offering the most generous diplomatic terms since the 1979 revolution. A policy of regime change became one of accommodation. Although the memorandum of understanding was short-lived—each side blames the other for abrogating it—the lesson Tehran learned was unmistakable: restraint projects weakness, whereas aggression is rewarded.

It has been revealed that “We seize concessions not through dialogue, but with missiles,” declared Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, a former IRGC commander, the current speaker of the parliament, and one of the regime’s most powerful figures. “The winner of any agreement,” he added, “is the one who is better prepared for war from the day after.” Tehran is already signaling that its chief postwar priority will not be to rebuild its decimated economy, but to restore—and expand—its ability to impose costs on its adversaries.

Recent findings suggest that the Strait of Hormuz offers the clearest example of this dynamic. What was once an Iranian threat has become, in Tehran’s eyes, an entitlement: the ability to regulate passage through one of the world’s most consequential energy chokepoints. For Iran, this constitutes both economic leverage and a potential deterrent against future attacks on itself and its regional proxies. For the rest of the world, it creates the prospect that Tehran can hold global energy markets hostage whenever it chooses.

According to recent reports, before the war, the Iranian regime’s longtime ambitions to drive the United States from the Middle East and end Israel’s existence appeared fanciful. Today, the growing number of American politicians and commentators who have called for the United States to end its aid to Israel and wind down its regional military presence has emboldened Tehran to believe it is winning the ideological war. “POTUS clearly recognizes that the vast majority of Americans are disgusted with Israel,” Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi remarked in a post on social media in November. He continued: “Americans are evidently sick and tired of Israel bamboozling US administrations into Forever Wars. They had enough. So has our region.”.

Sources indicate that the Islamic Republic’s newfound confidence is partly rooted in its ability to inflict enormous damage at comparatively little cost. Its Persian Gulf neighbors have spent decades and trillions of dollars transforming themselves into global hubs of energy, transportation, finance, and technology. And Iran can now threaten all of it with cheap Shahed drones against which the United States and its partners must field multimillion-dollar interceptors—a costly undertaking that Nick Carter, a retired British general and former chief of the British defense staff, likened to “Ferraris being thrown at Frisbees.” Building is costly and slow; destruction is fast and cheap. Rezaei has pledged to target undersea cables, data centers, and artificial intelligence facilities across the Gulf in the event of renewed fighting.

It has been revealed that the Islamic Republic’s theory of victory does not require defeating the United States militarily. It only requires persuading two audiences—the American public and Iran’s Gulf neighbors—that the U.S. military presence in the region and the partnership with Israel bring more harm than good. The attacks on American bases, Gulf data centers, and ships passing through the Strait of Hormuz are a message that the road to regional security must go through Iran, not the United States or Israel. “The nations and territories of the region will no longer serve as a shield for American bases,” Mojtaba Khamenei has declared.

Recent findings suggest that but this Iranian aggression is likely to produce the opposite of what it intends. Tehran’s threats against the Gulf only stoke the anxieties that sustain Washington’s military presence in the region. The result is a self-perpetuating cycle in which Gulf governments seek American protection against Iran, Tehran attempts to evict Washington from the region, and each new round of conflict deepens the Gulf states’ dependence on the United States.

Iran’s confrontation with Israel poses a different, potentially more explosive danger. The regime’s hostility to Israel has survived the destruction of much of Tehran’s military infrastructure and its regional proxy network. Iranian leaders remain determined to rebuild their missile and drone arsenals, restore the capabilities of allies such as Hezbollah, and avenge the killing of Ali Khamenei. Yet Israel is equally determined to prevent Iran from reconstituting the capabilities that threatened it before the war. Each side may therefore interpret the other’s attempts at deterrence as preparations for another attack.

According to recent reports, as for Trump’s original justification for the war—to avert an Iranian nuclear bomb—his actions and words have persuaded a growing number of Iranian officials to openly advocate nuclear arms development. The president himself supplied Tehran’s talking points. “If they had a nuclear weapon,” Trump told a crowd of supporters six months into the war, “I’d be calling the supreme leader and I’d be saying: ‘Mr. Supreme Leader, how are you, sir? Is there anything we can do for you?’—as opposed to bombing the crap out of him.”.

Recent findings suggest that since the 1979 revolution, Washington has tended to underestimate the Islamic Republic’s agency and overestimate its own ability to shape Iran’s future. Advocates of engagement often blame American hostility for Tehran’s intransigence, while advocates of confrontation have blamed American weakness. One side has overestimated the Islamic Republic’s flexibility; the other, its fragility. Both have been susceptible to what the former U.S. national security adviser H. R. McMaster has called “strategic narcissism”: the assumption that adversaries are primarily reacting to the United States rather than acting on their own interests, identities, and ambitions.

Industry observers note that trump’s war exposed the limits of trying both to bomb Iran into submission and to bribe it into moderation. In the span of four months, Washington employed overwhelming military force to weaken or overthrow the Islamic Republic, then offered sweeping economic and diplomatic incentives to alter its behavior. Neither altered a revolutionary stance that has been remarkably consistent for decades. As Henry Kissinger wrote in 1957, “The distinguishing feature of a revolutionary power is not that it feels threatened . . . but that nothing can reassure it.”.

According to recent reports, the seeds of the next war have already been planted. Regardless of what the United States chooses to do, the Islamic Republic’s renewed confidence, along with its resolve to rebuild its military might and retaliate for the death of its supreme leader, portends another showdown with Israel. Each side now views the other as an existential threat, and there is no direct channel of dialogue to prevent miscalculation and a potentially even more destructive war. For Washington, the implication is clear: The United States may seek to disengage from the Middle East, but it cannot insulate itself from the consequences of another war between Iran and Israel.

In a recent development, the Islamic Republic’s most consequential compromises came in 1988, when Khomeini reluctantly accepted a cease-fire ending the eight-year war with Iraq, and in 2015, when Iran agreed to stringent restrictions on its nuclear program. Although separated by nearly three decades, both decisions followed a similar logic. Faced with overwhelming pressure, international isolation, and a diplomatic off-ramp that does not require it to change its identity, the Islamic Republic has demonstrated a capacity to make concessions—but only in the service of living to fight another day.

In a recent development, in a 2013 speech foreshadowing Tehran’s nuclear compromise, Ali Khamenei described this approach as “heroic flexibility.” The supreme leader likened the regime to a wrestler who “indicates flexibility for technical reasons” but must never “forget who his opponent is and what he is doing.” Tactical flexibility, Khamenei insisted, must never come at the expense of Iran’s “revolutionary nature”: “The fact that the world has changed cannot give us an excuse to change our behavior, our ideals, and our goals.” Ali Khamenei had the legitimacy to push for heroic flexibility. The current regime is filled with men who will pursue escalation long before they ever call for compromise.

According to recent reports, today, the challenges posed by Iran are much greater than a decade ago. Washington must not only prevent it from acquiring nuclear weapons but also deter it from attacking its neighbors, disrupting the global energy trade through the Strait of Hormuz, and waging AI-assisted cyberwarfare and influence operations against the United States and its partners. At the same time, Washington has fewer allies and less diplomatic leverage than it did in 2015, and the trust gap between the two governments may prove unbridgeable. The Iranian regime believes that global public opinion is on its side, not Trump’s.

Recent findings suggest that the 48-year history of U.S. policy toward the Islamic Republic highlights that grand designs, whether for regime change or rapprochement, have failed. On two occasions, in 1988 and 2015, both sides reached narrow agreements that addressed Tehran’s conduct rather than its character. Lasting change, however, can come only from within Iran, when the pillars that sustain the Islamic Republic—a cohesive elite, a loyal coercive apparatus, and the absence of rival centers of power—crack. Rather than widening those cracks, Trump’s war may have narrowed them.

Sources indicate that iran’s rulers see the regime’s survival as proof of their own strength. Yet each crisis they weather leaves the country poorer, its people more estranged, and the regime more dependent on brutality to endure. Like Washington before it, Tehran now overestimates what force can achieve; its hubris may help produce the next war, just as the repression that quelled the last uprising will invariably fuel another. The revolutionary ideology that keeps the regime afloat will continue to weigh Iran down, leaving in place a leadership even more intent on resisting its adversaries, at home and abroad, than on governing its people. The regime may declare victory, but for the proud people of Iran—an ancient civilization and an energy superpower with a worthless currency, a shunned passport, and a leader in hiding—there is little reason to celebrate. What has not killed the Islamic Republic is slowly killing Iran.

KARIM SADJADPOUR is a Senior Fellow at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace.

Welcome to Foreign Policy’s Southeast Asia Brief.

Recent findings suggest that the highlights this week: What the ICJ’s genocide ruling means for Myanmar, a flurry of trade deals in the region, and new U.S. chip controls threatening Malaysian and Thai business.

ICJ: Myanmar Committed Genocide.

The state of Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya in 2017, the International Court of Justice (ICJ), the main judicial arm of the United Nations, ruled last Thursday.

Industry observers note that the ruling documents how, following attacks by the Arakan Rohingya Salvation Army (ARSA), Myanmar carried out a campaign of genocidal violence against the Rohingya. It estimates that 10,000 Rohingya, about 1.2 percent of the total population, were killed.

The court ruled 9-6 that the “only reasonable inference” was that this violence showed genocidal intent to destroy the Rohingya as a group—not just drive them out of Myanmar or exact collective punishment.

The ruling orders Myanmar to cease violence against the group and prosecute those responsible, allow the safe return of Rohingya to their homes, and pay compensation.

Recent findings suggest that sadly, none of this is likely. The junta has rejected the judgment as “unfair.”.

Meanwhile, another armed group called the Arakan Army, which controls most of Rakhine province and mainly represents ethnic Rakhine Buddhists, has also committed large-scale violence against the Rohingya. Fighting between the Arakan Army and Rohingya militant groups—which has seen the Rohingya militants, including the ARSA, occasionally cooperate with the junta—has added to the hostility.

The Arakan Army has made some overtures to Muslim communities in the province.

For now, though, the Arakan Army is taking a wait-and-see attitude to the ICJ judgment. A spokesperson told local media, “We are constantly monitoring the current developments. We will stand firmly on truth and justice and take appropriate action for the benefit of the Arakan region.”.

The country’s National Unity Government (NUG)—representing the civilian government overthrown by the junta in 2021 and associated with some of the main rebel forces—endorsed the judgment.

This was not a given. When Aung San Suu Kyi, an icon of the NUG, was acting as the country’s de facto leader, Myanmar consistently denied that the military’s actions against the Rohingya constituted a genocide.

In a recent development, in opposition, the NUG may now find its position easier. Its statement focused heavily on the junta’s culpability.

Recent findings suggest that but it may find the whole judgment hard to accept. The ruling finds the state of Myanmar—not just the military—guilty of genocide. And at that time when the most severe offense took place, in 2016 and 2017, the paramount power in the state apparatus was Aung San Suu Kyi.

In Southeast Asia, could this be a stumbling block for junta leader Min Aung Hlang’s push for diplomatic normalization with the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN)?

It has been revealed that thailand—the most vocal advocate for Myanmar’s full readmission to ASEAN—looks unmoved. “Thailand must take the position that best serves the country,” Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul told reporters.

Thai Foreign Minister Sihasak Phuangketkeow argued that Thailand’s engagement did not contradict the ruling, as Thailand’s aim was to curb the current violence.

Meanwhile, two other countries—Malaysia and the Philippines—have issued official statements on the matter.

Malaysia’s brief statement remarked that it “respects the judgment.” The Philippines’ statement seemed a shade weaker, saying it “acknowledges the judgment” and, unlike Malaysia, does not mention the Rohingya by name.

Other ASEAN countries have yet to make official statements.

Still, for countries opposed to Myanmar’s full readmission to the bloc—most notably Singapore, which serves as the ASEAN chair next year—the judgment will reinforce this skepticism.

On the global stage, China has objected. “China has concerns over challenges such as overreach of jurisdiction and expansive interpretation, and believes such practices are not conducive to dispute resolution,” a spokesperson mentioned.

Recent findings suggest that regarding the United States, this judgment—plus the results of the country’s midterms—will likely impede the U.S. push toward normalization.

According to recent reports, parts of the American right reject the judgment. While the U.S. government declared in 2022that the anti-Rohingya violence constituted a genocide, some on the right are concerned that the ICJ judgments lay the groundwork for a finding of genocide against Israel, linked to its war in Gaza.

And the Myanmar junta clearly still thinks that it might find a sympathetic ear from the Trump administration.

Sources indicate that when objecting to the ICJ ruling, a spokesperson for the Myanmar military cited a recent joint statement by U.S. President Donald Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping, and Russian President Vladimir Putin that the International Criminal Court “must not abuse” its jurisdiction.

While the International Criminal Court is distinct from the ICJ, the spokesperson for Ming Aung Hlaing drew a parallel.

It has been revealed that trump deals details. On Thursday evening, the White House disclosed the details of some of the various deals struck at last week’s ASEAN summit.

The ASEAN deals, worth a total of $17 billion, include a $12 billion sale of Boeing aircraft to Philippine Airlines.

The United States is also looking at providing $2 billion in loans for Philippine defense purchases and $400 million in military financing (though much of the funding was already committed).

Thailand will also purchase $123 million of High Mobility Artillery Rocket Systems (HIMARS) from the United States.

Industry observers note that the terms of the Thai deal, which are not yet final, are already provoking opposition there. Many in the agricultural powerhouse are unhappy with the prospect of more agricultural imports from the United States—in particular, pork. The government is on the defense, saying that it’s the best deal it could get.

Amid controversy over the price tag, Thailand has also insisted that the HIMARS purchase is unrelated to the trade deal and was driven by national security considerations.

It has been revealed that the Malaysian government also unveiled that a U.S. consortium will help develop a sovereign artificial intelligence cloud for the Malaysian government, with the United States offering $50 million in support.

EU-Indonesia trade deal. On Saturday, the European Union and Indonesia signed a trade deal that was 10 years in the making.

Under the terms of the deal, both sides will remove import duties on about 90 percent of products, including EU automotives and most agricultural exports. The products not included will see their tariffs gradually reduced or receive tariff-free quotas.

According to recent reports, indonesia expects that clothing, footwear, and palm oil will receive the biggest export boosts. It also hopes that the deal will boost European investment in Indonesia in sectors such as critical minerals, batteries, electric vehicles, pharmaceuticals, and electronics.

The deal also addresses a substantial number of nontariff barriers that often bedevil foreign products entering Indonesia.

The EU’s rules on deforestation, long a sticking point for Indonesia, have been finessed. While Indonesia did not secure an exemption, the EU left the door open to accepting Indonesia’s domestic standards.

In a recent development, the deal comes as both the EU and Indonesia are looking to expand their global trade partnerships to offset U.S. tariffs.

Even more deals. The Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in China last week also saw a flurry of dealmaking.

Singaporean Prime Minister Lawrence Wong and Xi met and unveiled negotiations to upgrade the two country’s free trade agreement.

Indonesia and China said they will launch formal negotiations for a comprehensive economic partnership.

They also declared strategic partnerships worth $71.8 billion, including the development of 10 “smart cities” by a partnership between Indonesian state-asset fund Danantara and a Chinese state-owned enterprise as well as deals involving a Chinese appliance maker and a consortium of other Chinese organizations investing $20 billion, also in partnership with Danantara.

Meanwhile, Vietnam unveiled plans to deepen energy cooperation with Russia in both fossil fuels and nuclear energy.

Huang’s Return Is the Biggest National Security Scandal in U.S. History by James Palmer.

The Middle East Is Finally on Its Own by Stephen M. Walt.

Shenzhen Was No Yalta Conference by James Palmer.

Elon Musk is quietly developing a couple of islands in the Philippines, reported by Gabryelle Dumalag in the Philippine Daily Inquirer.

Malaysians turn to professional ticket concierges to secure seats at hot events, Norman Goh reports in Nikkei Asia.

With the president’s popularity sinking, political parties are dodging the VP nomination in Indonesia, an editorial in Tempo.

Last week, shortly before Trump jetted off to the Philippines and then China, the United States announced newly introduced controls on chip exports following the Jensen Huang scandal.

A license is now needed to export, reexport, or transfer advanced semiconductors to five countries: Brazil, Indonesia, Singapore, Malaysia, and Thailand.

Additionally, data centers, foreign foundries, and chip exports are expected to perform due diligence to check if their customers are owned or controlled by U.S.-embargoed destinations—China, in this case.

And the measures close the loophole of selling chips to data centers outside of China that provide processing power to companies in China.

Recent findings suggest that for countries that have been cashing in on the AI boom, this represents a major challenge. Southeast Asia has emerged as major data center hub. The latest regulations will disrupt this.

At least two partners of Nvidia that design equipment used in data centers powered by its chips have suspended shipments to Southeast Asia, according to reporting by Nikkei Asia.

Nikkei Asia also reported that Taiwanese chipmaker Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company has already put several orders by Chinese and non-Chinese customers on hold. The regulations are so strict that they threaten to disrupt not just data centers but also smartphones, consumer electronics, and autonomous cars produced in Southeast Asia’s major electronics industry.

In Malaysia, tech stocks sold off sharply in reaction to the news. Industry players also worried that it could seriously impact the country’s chip design industry.

Thai business, meanwhile, is concerned that the regulations could put the brakes on the country’s booming data center industry.

Reactions by governments have been mixed. Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim complained in an interview with the South China Morning Post that the United States was harder to work with than China, as the latter did not pick sides.

Wong, the Singaporean prime minister, signaled a potential crackdown, saying that countries “abusing Singapore’s trusted position” to circumvent export controls was a “real concern.” However, he also made clear that Singapore expected to still work with both the United States and China.

But hovering over all of this is this question: Will these rules last?

Huang is now back at Nvidia, backed by Trump. The president, it seems—despite the best efforts of his administration’s hawks—remains unconvinced by chip controls.

Joseph Rachman is the writer of Foreign Policy’s weekly Southeast Asia Brief. He is a freelance journalist based in Bangkok. X: @rachman_joseph.

💡 Key Takeaways
